Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiBleed distributed credential stuffing against FortiGate SSL VPN ending in successful auth · [LLM] Successful FortiGate VPN/admin login to default or built-in Fortinet accounts from public IP · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-VPN lateral movement: FortiGate-authenticated account fans out across internal Windows hosts · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
FortiBleed distributed credential stuffing against FortiGate SSL VPN ending in successful auth AIExploitation High
Hunts the FortiBleed signature of high-volume SSL VPN authentication failures (logid 0101039426 / ssl-login-fail) sprayed from many distinct source IPs against a single FortiGate, followed by at least one successful tunnel-up for the same appliance/user. Distinguishes the campaign's fully-automated leaked-password spray from a single fat-fingered user. Rationale: Uses the article's exact attack shape (mass spray of leaked Fortinet passwords from many IPs) plus the corroborated FortiGate logid 0101039426 / ssl-login-fail string; the failure-volume + distinct-source + same-appliance-success correlation is what turns noisy VPN brute force into a confirmed FortiBleed compromise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/06/18/cisa-urges-hardening-fortinet-devices-after-reports-credential-exposure • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://community.fortinet.com/t5/FortiGate/Technical-Tip-SSL-VPN-Brute-Force-or-Multiple-Unknown-Failed/ta-p/366773
ATT&CKT1110.004 T1110.003 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user repeatedly fat-fingering an expired password from a single corporate egress IP (won't trip the >=10 distinct-source threshold)
  • Internal vulnerability scanner / pentest authenticating against the VPN portal
  • Misconfigured MDM or VPN client looping reconnection attempts after a password change
  • Shared NAT egress where many real users fail at once during an outage
  • Security team running an authorized credential-validation exercise
Suppression filter
| where not (DistinctSrcIPs == 1)  // single-IP failure storms are usually a broken client, not the distributed FortiBleed spray
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the SuccessUsers/SuccessSrcIPs for the appliance — confirm whether the successful login source IP overlaps the spraying IP set and whether the account is a generic/built-in one. Check geolocation and prior login history for that account. 2) CONTAIN: Per CISA guidance, terminate all active SSL VPN and admin sessions on that FortiGate, force-reset the compromised account's password, and block the spraying source IPs at the edge. 3) HUNT: Review whether the now-authenticated session pivoted inward (see the post-VPN lateral-movement UC), audit FortiGate config for unauthorized changes, and confirm the appliance is on FortiOS 7.2.11/7.4.8/7.6.1+ with PBKDF2 hashing enabled.
let lookback = 24h;
let failThreshold = 30;      // >=30 failed SSL VPN auths against one appliance
let srcThreshold = 10;       // from >=10 distinct source IPs = distributed spray, not one user
let Fail = CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
  | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
  | where Activity has "ssl-login-fail" or DeviceEventClassID == "0101039426" or Message has "ssl-login-fail"
  | summarize Failures=count(), DistinctSrcIPs=dcount(SourceIP), TargetedUsers=make_set(DestinationHostName,50), SrcIPs=make_set(SourceIP,50), FirstFail=min(TimeGenerated), LastFail=max(TimeGenerated) by Appliance=DeviceExternalID
  | where Failures >= failThreshold and DistinctSrcIPs >= srcThreshold;
let Success = CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
  | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
  | where Message has "tunnel-up" or Activity has "tunnel-up" or DeviceEventClassID == "0101039947"
  | summarize SuccessCount=count(), SuccessUsers=make_set(DestinationHostName,50), SuccessSrcIPs=make_set(SourceIP,50), FirstSuccess=min(TimeGenerated) by Appliance=DeviceExternalID;
Fail
| join kind=inner Success on Appliance
| where FirstSuccess between (FirstFail .. LastFail + 1h)
| project Appliance, Failures, DistinctSrcIPs, TargetedUsers, SrcIPs, SuccessCount, SuccessUsers, SuccessSrcIPs, FirstFail, LastFail, FirstSuccess
| sort by Failures desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true count as failures, dc(Authentication.src) as failed_src_ips, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where (Authentication.vendor_product="Fortinet*" OR Authentication.app IN ("ssl-vpn","sslvpn")) Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.dest, Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where failures>=30 AND failed_src_ips>=10 | join type=inner dest user [ | tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true count as successes, values(Authentication.src) as success_src from datamodel=Authentication where (Authentication.vendor_product="Fortinet*" OR Authentication.app IN ("ssl-vpn","sslvpn")) Authentication.action=success by Authentication.dest, Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` ] | where successes>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true count as failures, dc(Authentication.src) as failed_src_ips, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where (Authentication.vendor_product="Fortinet*" OR Authentication.app IN ("ssl-vpn","sslvpn")) Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.dest, Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where failures>=30 AND failed_src_ips>=10 | join type=inner dest user [ | tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true count as successes, values(Authentication.src) as success_src from datamodel=Authentication where (Authentication.vendor_product="Fortinet*" OR Authentication.app IN ("ssl-vpn","sslvpn")) Authentication.action=success by Authentication.dest, Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` ] | where successes>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - failures
Successful FortiGate VPN/admin login to default or built-in Fortinet accounts from public IP AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful FortiGate authentications to generic admin or built-in Fortinet system accounts (admin, fortinet, maintainer, etc.) from an external/public source IP. SOCRadar attributes 63%+ of FortiBleed-compromised credentials to unrenamed default and built-in accounts, so a valid login to one of these from the internet is a direct campaign indicator even with zero preceding failures. Rationale: Built directly on the SOCRadar finding that generic admin (35%) and built-in Fortinet (28.3%) accounts dominate the compromised credential set, combined with a public-source-IP filter and the GreyNoise-corroborated target username list (admin/administrador/vpn/vpnuser); a successful external login to a never-renamed default account is high-fidelity for FortiBleed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://community.fortinet.com/t5/FortiGate/Technical-Tip-SSL-VPN-Brute-Force-or-Multiple-Unknown-Failed/ta-p/366773 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/06/18/cisa-urges-hardening-fortinet-devices-after-reports-credential-exposure
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1078 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organization legitimately uses an account literally named 'admin' for break-glass remote management (should be renamed per CISA)
  • MSP / vendor support logging into the firewall remotely with a shared admin account
  • Out-of-band management from an admin's home/cellular IP that geolocates as public
  • Monitoring or backup-config tooling authenticating with a 'report' or 'operator' service account over the internet
  • Test/lab FortiGate intentionally exposed with default credentials
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("")  // replace with allowlist of known MSP/admin egress IPs once baselined; keep all public IPs in scope until then
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Verify the AuthUser is actually a default/built-in account and not a renamed equivalent; check whether the SourceIP is known-good admin egress or a fresh foreign IP, and whether MFA was satisfied. 2) CONTAIN: Disable or rename the account, rotate its credential, terminate the active session, and restrict the management/VPN interface to known admin source ranges. 3) HUNT: Pull all actions taken in that session (config edits, new admin creation, VPN policy changes) and pivot to the lateral-movement UC to see if internal hosts were reached from the assigned VPN IP.
let lookback = 24h;
let defaultAccounts = dynamic(["admin","administrator","administrador","fortinet","fortigate","maintainer","user","vpn","vpnuser","guest","report","operator","super_admin"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
| where DeviceEventClassID in ("0100032002","0101039947") or Message has "tunnel-up" or (Activity has "login" and Message has "success")
| extend AuthUser = tolower(coalesce(DestinationHostName, SourceUserName))
| where AuthUser in (defaultAccounts)
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
| project TimeGenerated, Appliance = DeviceExternalID, AuthUser, SourceIP, Activity, DeviceEventClassID, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true count, values(Authentication.src) as src, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.vendor_product="Fortinet*" Authentication.user IN ("admin","administrator","administrador","fortinet","fortigate","maintainer","user","vpn","vpnuser","guest","report","operator","super_admin") by Authentication.dest, Authentication.user, Authentication.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | iplocation src | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | table firstTime, lastTime, dest, user, src, Country, count | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true count, values(Authentication.src) as src, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.vendor_product="Fortinet*" Authentication.user IN ("admin","administrator","administrador","fortinet","fortigate","maintainer","user","vpn","vpnuser","guest","report","operator","super_admin") by Authentication.dest, Authentication.user, Authentication.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | iplocation src | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | table firstTime, lastTime, dest, user, src, Country, count | sort - count
Post-VPN lateral movement: FortiGate-authenticated account fans out across internal Windows hosts AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a successful FortiGate SSL VPN authentication with the same account performing successful network logons to many distinct internal Windows hosts shortly after — the corroborated FortiBleed second stage where stolen VPN access is used to move laterally, extract NTLM hashes and run Kerberos attacks against Windows domains. Anchored on the VPN account so it targets the campaign, not generic admin activity. Rationale: Implements the corroborated FortiBleed second stage (SecurityWeek/Windows News: stolen VPN access -> NTLM hash extraction and Kerberos attacks on Windows domains) by anchoring on the VPN account name and requiring distinct-host fan-out within hours of the VPN tunnel-up, which is what separates attacker pivoting from a legitimate remote admin. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/cisa-issues-emergency-warning-as-fortibleed-exploits-fortigate-ssl-vpn-credentials-to-target-windows.427882 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/06/18/cisa-urges-hardening-fortinet-devices-after-reports-credential-exposure
ATT&CKT1078 T1021.002 T1550.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate domain or helpdesk admin connecting via VPN then RDP/SMB-ing to many servers for maintenance
  • Vulnerability scanner or asset-inventory tool running authenticated scans from a VPN-connected account
  • Backup or patch-management service account that touches many hosts over the network
  • SCCM/Intune or monitoring agents authenticating across the fleet under a shared account
  • DFS/file-share replication generating broad network logons for a service identity
Suppression filter
| where AcctLower !in ("svc-backup","svc-scanner","svc-sccm")  // baseline-then-exclude known broad-access service accounts; keep human/admin accounts in scope
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the account is a real human/service identity and whether the VPN source IP is expected; review the reached host list for crown-jewel servers and domain controllers, and check 4624 LogonType/AuthenticationPackage for NTLM vs Kerberos anomalies. 2) CONTAIN: Disable the account, kill the VPN session, and isolate any host where credential-dumping or Kerberos abuse is evident. 3) HUNT: Look for 4768/4769 Kerberos anomalies, LSASS access, and new local admin/service creation on the touched hosts; rotate KRBTGT and affected service-account passwords if NTLM/Kerberos abuse is confirmed.
let lookback = 24h;
let vpnWindow = 4h;          // lateral activity within 4h of the VPN auth
let hostFanout = 5;          // >=5 distinct internal hosts reached = fan-out, not normal use
let VpnLogon = CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
  | where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" and DeviceProduct has "Fortigate"
  | where Message has "tunnel-up" or DeviceEventClassID == "0101039947"
  | extend VpnUser = tolower(coalesce(DestinationHostName, SourceUserName))
  | where isnotempty(VpnUser)
  | project VpnTime = TimeGenerated, VpnUser, VpnSrcIP = SourceIP;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where EventID == 4624 and LogonType == 3
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
| extend AcctLower = tolower(TargetUserName)
| join kind=inner VpnLogon on $left.AcctLower == $right.VpnUser
| where TimeGenerated between (VpnTime .. VpnTime + vpnWindow)
| summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(Computer), Hosts=make_set(Computer,50), LogonCount=count(), FirstLateral=min(TimeGenerated) by AcctLower, VpnSrcIP, VpnTime
| where DistinctHosts >= hostFanout
| sort by DistinctHosts desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true min(_time) as vpnTime, values(Authentication.src) as vpn_src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.vendor_product="Fortinet*" Authentication.app IN ("ssl-vpn","sslvpn") by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | rename user as account | join type=inner account [ | tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true dc(Authentication.dest) as host_count, values(Authentication.dest) as hosts, min(_time) as firstLateral from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.vendor_product="Microsoft*" by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | rename user as account ] | where host_count>=5 AND firstLateral>=vpnTime | convert ctime(vpnTime) ctime(firstLateral) | table account, vpn_src, vpnTime, firstLateral, host_count, hosts | sort - host_count
| tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true min(_time) as vpnTime, values(Authentication.src) as vpn_src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.vendor_product="Fortinet*" Authentication.app IN ("ssl-vpn","sslvpn") by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | rename user as account | join type=inner account [ | tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true dc(Authentication.dest) as host_count, values(Authentication.dest) as hosts, min(_time) as firstLateral from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.vendor_product="Microsoft*" by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | rename user as account ] | where host_count>=5 AND firstLateral>=vpnTime | convert ctime(vpnTime) ctime(firstLateral) | table account, vpn_src, vpnTime, firstLateral, host_count, hosts | sort - host_count
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Network-AI sandbox escape: node spawns /bin/sh -c with allowlist prefix + shell metacharacter injection · [LLM] Network-AI CVE-2026-54051 proof-of-concept artifact execution (poc-316.js / PWNED-316.txt) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-54051: Network-AI: Improper Neutralization of Special

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Network-AI CVE-2026-54051 post-exploit: Linux recon utilities spawned from shell child of node
Network-AI sandbox escape: node spawns /bin/sh -c with allowlist prefix + shell metacharacter injection AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-54051 core exploit: the network-ai SandboxPolicy allowlist glob-matches the whole command string but ShellExecutor runs it via /bin/sh -c, so an allowed prefix (git/npm/node/yarn/pnpm) followed by ;, &&, ||, $() or backticks becomes arbitrary execution. Surfaces a node parent spawning a shell with -c where the command line carries both an allowlisted prefix and an unquoted shell metacharacter. Rationale: Uses the exact mechanism named in the article — node/npm/git/yarn/pnpm allowlist prefixes glob-matched whole-string, executed through /bin/sh -c, plus the article's enumerated metacharacter set (; & | $ ` ( ) < > { }). The node-parent + sh -c + prefix + metachar combination is the article's primary exploit (UC_12_2).
ATT&CKT1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm lifecycle scripts that chain shell commands with && (e.g. "build && test")
  • CI/CD runners (Jenkins, GitLab runner) invoking node tooling that shells out
  • pm2 / nodemon process managers launching shell wrappers
  • Developer running a node script that calls git with a $(...) subshell
  • Postinstall hooks combining multiple commands with ;
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run","npm exec","yarn run","node_modules/.bin") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("&&","||") and not ProcessCommandLine has_any ("id;","whoami","/tmp/","curl ","wget ","nc "))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent node command line; identify whether the shell payload follows a legitimate allowlist prefix and whether the metacharacter introduces an unrelated command (id, curl, nc) vs a benign build chain. 2) Contain: if the host runs network-ai < 5.9.1 and the injected segment is non-build (recon/network), isolate the host and kill the orchestrator process; capture /proc and any dropped marker files. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same node parent for child recon binaries and outbound connections; check for network-ai version and remove broad wildcard allowlist entries (node */npm *).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-c"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\b(git|npm|node|yarn|pnpm)\b"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"[;&|`$(){}<>]"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-c"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\b(git|npm|node|yarn|pnpm)\b"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"[;&|`$(){}<>]"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network-AI CVE-2026-54051 post-exploit: Linux recon utilities spawned from shell child of node AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the post-exploitation enumeration that follows a successful CVE-2026-54051 allowlist bypass: a shell (sh/bash/dash) whose parent is node executing reconnaissance binaries. Fires when the orchestrator-spawned shell runs id, whoami, uname, hostname, curl, wget, nc, ncat, python, perl, ssh-keygen or cat. Rationale: Maps the article's post-exploitation profile (id ran via the injected /bin/sh -c in the PoC) and the reviewer-supplied recon binary set, scoped to a node grandparent in Defender/Falcon where InitiatingProcessParentFileName is available. Sentinel ImProcessCreate exposes only parent (sh) so the node grandparent constraint is relaxed there.
ATT&CKT1033 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based deploy scripts legitimately calling curl/wget to fetch artifacts
  • Healthcheck wrappers running id/whoami/hostname inside containers
  • CI jobs invoking python via a shell step
  • Admin troubleshooting scripts under a node-managed service
  • Container entrypoint shells gathering uname/hostname at startup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/healthcheck","/entrypoint","deploy.sh") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the grandparent is the network-ai orchestrator node process and the recon command was not part of a known deploy/healthcheck script; review the preceding sh -c command line for an injected metacharacter. 2) Contain: if recon is paired with outbound nc/curl/wget to an untrusted host, isolate the device and snapshot the process tree and any written files. 3) Hunt: search the same host/account for the allowlist-bypass parent event (UC1), outbound C2, ssh-keygen output, and credential file reads; verify network-ai is upgraded to >= 5.9.1.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "node"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash")
| where FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","ssh-keygen","cat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","ssh-keygen","cat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network-AI CVE-2026-54051 proof-of-concept artifact execution (poc-316.js / PWNED-316.txt) AIExploitation High
Hunts for execution or file activity referencing the published CVE-2026-54051 PoC artifacts — the poc-316.js exploit script and its PWNED-316.txt success marker. A direct, high-fidelity indicator of active testing or exploitation of the network-ai allowlist bypass. Rationale: Targets the literal exploit artifacts named in the article PoC (`node poc-316.js`, marker `PWNED-316.txt`). These strings are unique to CVE-2026-54051 testing, giving a very low-FP alerting signal across process and file telemetry.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally validating the patch by running the published PoC
  • A vulnerability scanner or red-team toolkit shipping poc-316.js
  • A file named poc-316.js committed to an internal research repo and opened by an editor
  • Mirror/backup process copying a saved copy of the advisory PoC
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host belongs to an authorised security/red-team tester; check the parent process (node) and whether PWNED-316.txt was actually written. 2) Contain: on a non-authorised host, isolate it, preserve poc-316.js and any marker file, and kill the network-ai orchestrator process. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1/UC2 on the same host/account for the allowlist-bypass parent and post-exploit recon; confirm network-ai is upgraded to >= 5.9.1 and remove wildcard allowlist entries.

Vulnerable network-ai (<=5.7.1) npm package present in node_modules AIDelivery High
Asset-inventory hunt that surfaces hosts with the vulnerable Jovancoding/Network-AI package on disk (CVE-2026-48814 / CVE-2026-46701). The package files land under node_modules\network-ai; presence is the precondition for the unauthenticated MCP SSE exposure. Triage version against the 5.7.2 fixed release. Rationale: Pivots on the concrete install path 'node_modules\network-ai' named in the advisory (bin/mcp-server.ts, lib/mcp-transport-sse.ts live under it). Cache-path exclusions cut npm/pnpm store noise so only real project installs surface for remediation against the 5.7.2 fix. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/network-ai/CVE-2026-46701/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-48814-cwe-306-missing-authentication-for--a37c283f4afc7554 • https://www.squaredtech.co/mcp-security-flaw-npm-package-ships-with-no-auth-by-default
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstation with network-ai intentionally installed for legitimate multi-agent orchestration
  • CI/CD build agent pulling the package during npm/pnpm install for tests
  • Security researcher detonating the package in a sandbox
  • Already-remediated 5.7.2+ install (identical path, patched version — verify package.json version field)
  • Monorepo with nested node_modules copies inflating host count
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"_cacache" and FolderPath !has @"\.npm\" and FolderPath !has @"\pnpm-store\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open package.json under the flagged node_modules\network-ai path and read the version; if >=5.7.2 it is patched — close. If <=5.7.1, confirm whether the host runs the SSE MCP server (see companion process UC). 2) Contain: have the owner upgrade to network-ai 5.7.2+, or if the server is running, set a non-empty NETWORK_AI_MCP_SECRET and rebind the listener to 127.0.0.1 until patched. 3) Hunt: pivot the host into the process-launch and inbound-POST UCs to determine whether the vulnerable SSE server was ever started or reached from a non-loopback source.

| where FolderPath has @"node_modules\network-ai"
| where FolderPath !has @"_cacache" and FolderPath !has @"\.npm\" and FolderPath !has @"\pnpm-store\"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), FilesWritten=dcount(FileName), SamplePath=any(FolderPath), SawPackageJson=maxif(1, FileName =~ "package.json") by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), FilesWritten=dcount(TargetFileName), SamplePath=any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc

network-ai MCP SSE server launched in non-stdio (vulnerable) mode AIInstallation High
Detects process creation of the Network-AI MCP server (command line contains both 'network-ai' and 'mcp-server') without the --stdio flag, i.e. the SSE listener that ships with the empty-default-secret authorization bypass. Stdio-mode invocations are excluded because the advisory's only safe path requires --stdio. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact invocation tokens — the 'network-ai' package and its 'mcp-server' bin — and excludes --stdio, the only mode the advisory deems non-vulnerable. Surfaces the listening SSE server before exploitation rather than a generic node process. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/network-ai/CVE-2026-46701/ • https://www.squaredtech.co/mcp-security-flaw-npm-package-ships-with-no-auth-by-default
ATT&CKT1059 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator running the server locally bound to 127.0.0.1 for legitimate single-user use
  • Developer testing network-ai during feature work
  • Automated integration-test harness spinning the server up and tearing it down
  • Patched 5.7.2+ host where the secret is now enforced (still launches the same process — confirm version)
  • Container entrypoint launching the SSE server with a properly set NETWORK_AI_MCP_SECRET
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the on-disk network-ai version (<=5.7.1 = exposed) and whether NETWORK_AI_MCP_SECRET is set in the service/unit/container env; an empty/unset secret means _isAuthorized() returns true for all callers. 2) Contain: stop the SSE listener or rebind it to loopback, set a strong NETWORK_AI_MCP_SECRET, and upgrade to 5.7.2+. 3) Hunt: pull DeviceNetworkEvents/web logs for this host and run the inbound-POST /mcp UC to see whether any non-loopback caller already reached config_set / agent_spawn / token_* tools.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "network-ai" and ProcessCommandLine has "mcp-server"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--stdio"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "network-ai" and CommandLine has "mcp-server"
| where CommandLine !has "--stdio"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated non-loopback POST /mcp tool invocation against network-ai SSE server AIExploitation Medium
Active-exploitation detection for CVE-2026-48814: a non-loopback caller (curl/SSRF/0.0.0.0 bind) issues POST /mcp to the Network-AI SSE server and gets HTTP 200 with no Authorization header, invoking MCP tools (config_set, agent_spawn, blackboard_write, token_*) against the empty default secret. Web/proxy logs carry the path+method+auth-header signal; EDR network telemetry carries the non-loopback inbound exposure. Rationale: Targets the advisory's PoC exactly — POST /mcp, HTTP 200, no auth, non-loopback source — using the web-log auth-header emptiness (ImWebSession.HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) as the unauthenticated signal, with EDR inbound-non-loopback as a corroborating exposure pivot when proxy logs are absent. Datadog left blank: no generic web-access-log source in this tenant's listed schema carries POST/path/auth-header. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/network-ai/CVE-2026-46701/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-48814-cwe-306-missing-authentication-for--a37c283f4afc7554 • https://www.squaredtech.co/mcp-security-flaw-npm-package-ships-with-no-auth-by-default
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner / ASM probing the /mcp endpoint
  • Authorized local MCP client legitimately sending no Authorization header because the secret was never configured (still the vuln — worth flagging)
  • Reverse-proxy or container health check polling /mcp
  • Container/NAT bridge rewriting a loopback request so it appears as a non-loopback SrcIpAddr
  • Load balancer or service mesh sidecar fronting the SSE server with stripped auth headers
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination host runs network-ai <=5.7.1 SSE mode, then inspect the request URL/body for invoked tool names (config_set, agent_spawn, blackboard_write, token_revoke) and check the source IP against known scanners and internal ranges. 2) Contain: block ingress to the MCP port from non-loopback sources at the host/SG firewall, set a strong NETWORK_AI_MCP_SECRET, restart the service, and upgrade to 5.7.2+. 3) Hunt: enumerate every POST /mcp 200 from this source across all hosts, review token_* and config_set invocations for tampering or stolen credentials, and rotate any tokens the blackboard/agent tools could have exposed.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "network-ai" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "mcp-server"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--stdio"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType != "Loopback" and RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Ports=make_set(LocalPort, 10) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/mcp"
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Salesforce REST API access with Python-urllib agent from integration identity (Icarus/UNC6395) AIExploitation High
Hunts non-human/integration identities authenticating to Salesforce and driving REST API calls with a raw Python-urllib user-agent. Legitimate Salesforce integrations (MuleSoft, Fivetran, OwnBackup, Data Loader) present named API clients; the bare python-urllib default UA is the common thread across the Icarus, ShinyHunters and Salesloft-Drift/UNC6395 OAuth-token data-theft campaigns. Rationale: Uses the article's high-fidelity 'Python-urllib user-agent' string (cross-confirmed by ReliaQuest and the UNC6395/Salesloft-Drift Google Cloud write-up) against the guaranteed CloudAppEvents.UserAgent column; a raw library UA from a CRM integration identity is anomalous by construction. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/klue-oauth-breach-linked-to-icarus-salesforce-data-theft-attacks/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1199 T1078.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal data-science / BI team pulling reports via a homegrown Python (urllib) script
  • QA or staging automation hitting a Salesforce sandbox with default UA
  • A legacy in-house ETL job that never set a named API client
  • Postman/curl-style ad-hoc admin testing that bundles urllib
  • Monitoring/uptime tooling polling a Salesforce health endpoint
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent matches regex @"(?i)\bpython-urllib/\d"   // require the raw library default UA, not a named client that merely embeds urllib
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the AccountId/AccountDisplayName and SourceIPs from the hit; confirm whether this is a sanctioned integration service account and whether its source IPs match the vendor's published egress ranges (Klue/MuleSoft/etc.). A service identity calling from datacenter/VPS IPs not on the allowlist is the red flag. 2) CONTAIN: In Salesforce Setup, revoke the OAuth token / connected-app session for that identity and reset the integration credential; block the source IPs at the org's Login IP Ranges / network. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC3 (bulk query burst) and UC2 (sobjects enumeration) for the same AccountId, and review what sObjects/records were returned to scope data exposure.

            Actions = make_set(ActionType, 15),

        by AccountId, AccountDisplayName, UserAgent
| order by ApiEvents desc

Salesforce object-catalog enumeration via /services/data/v59.0/sobjects AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the reconnaissance step where the actor enumerates the org's full sObject catalog through the Salesforce REST describe endpoint before bulk extraction. A trusted integration identity that suddenly walks the entire object schema is the precursor to the QueryMore extraction loop seen in the Icarus/Klue intrusion. Rationale: Pins on the exact REST recon endpoint named by ReliaQuest ('GET /services/data/v59.0/sobjects'); the URI string surfaces in CloudAppEvents.RawEventData / Web.url for Salesforce EventLogFile-sourced API activity, making this an article-specific discovery pivot rather than a generic API-usage dashboard. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/icarus-threat-actors-exploit-klue-oauth-breach-to-steal-salesforce-data
ATT&CKT1526 T1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A newly connected integration (Boomi/MuleSoft/Tableau) doing its first metadata describe of all objects
  • Salesforce admin or developer using Workbench / a schema-export tool
  • DevOps deployment tooling (Gearset/Copado) refreshing object metadata pre-release
  • Marketing Cloud / CDP connector syncing its object map
  • Backup tooling (OwnBackup) cataloging objects before a snapshot
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent has "urllib"   // tighten to the campaign automation UA; legitimate metadata-describe tools use named API clients
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the AccountId doing the describe-all and check whether a sObjects walk is expected for that identity (new integration onboarding vs. a long-lived account that has never enumerated before). First-time-ever enumeration by an established integration is suspicious. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned, revoke the connected-app token and the integration credential, and capture the source IPs for blocking. 3) HUNT: Immediately correlate forward in time (same AccountId/IP) for the /services/data/v59.0/query loop (UC3) — recon-then-bulk-query within the same session converts this from hunting to confirmed exfil.

Bulk Salesforce CRM extraction: high-volume /query + QueryMore loop from one identity AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the data-theft phase: a single Salesforce identity issuing a concentrated burst of REST query calls against /services/data/v59.0/query and paginating via QueryMore. ReliaQuest observed ~1,000 queries in 15 minutes and sustained 6-24h loops in the Icarus/Klue intrusion — a volume profile no human and few sanctioned jobs produce. Rationale: Encodes the article's quantified exfil signature (the /services/data/v59.0/query + QueryMore loop and the 'nearly a thousand queries in 15 minutes' burst from ReliaQuest) as a per-identity threshold; it is a temporal-volume detection that no single-event Sigma rule can express. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/klue-integration-breached-salesforce/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employees legitimately browsing the AU retail sites house.com.au, robinskitchen.com.au or baccarat.com.au (these are real homeware/cookware retailers that were compromised — expect heavy benign traffic, especially for AU-based orgs)
  • Legitimate use of gofile.io for sharing large files between colleagues/partners
  • Threat-intel or scanning platforms validating the IOC IPs from within the SOC range
  • A shared-hosting IP reassigned to a benign tenant after the campaign
  • Marketing/web teams checking competitor or supplier sites
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("house.com.au","robinskitchen.com.au","baccarat.com.au") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe"))   // drop user-driven browser hits to the compromised AU retail domains; keep IP hits, gofile.io, and non-browser process contexts
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For domain hits on the AU retail sites, treat browser-context connections as likely benign and prioritize non-interactive/server or scripted process contexts and any gofile.io upload; for the IP hits, confirm timing against the breach window (campaign active from 2026-04-28). 2) CONTAIN: Block the four IOC IPs and gofile.io at the proxy/firewall; for confirmed hits, isolate the host and capture the initiating process. 3) HUNT: Correlate any confirmed egress with Salesforce session source IPs (UC1/UC3) — a host or identity that both queried Salesforce in bulk and touched gofile.io is a strong exfil chain; review proxy bytes-out to gofile.io to estimate data volume.
let IocIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
let IocDomains = dynamic(["house.com.au","robinskitchen.com.au","baccarat.com.au","gofile.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (IocIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (IocDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let IocIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
let IocDomains = dynamic(["house.com.au","robinskitchen.com.au","baccarat.com.au","gofile.io"]);

   | where DstIpAddr in (IocIPs)

status: experimental
description: |

AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-19 7 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

AutoJack is a novel exploit chain showing how a single malicious webpage can turn an AI browsing agent into a remote code execution vector on the host machine. By abusing trust in localhost, missing authentication, and unsafe parameter handling, attackers can trigger arbitrary process execution through AutoGen Studio’s MCP WebSocket. The research highlights a broader pattern - when agents can browse untrusted content and access local services, traditional boundaries like localhost are no longer secure. The post AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent appeared first o…

ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1190 T1195.002 T1218.005 T1218.010 T1218.011

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AutoGen Studio browsing agent crosses loopback to MCP WebSocket (AutoJack) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AutoGen Studio (python) spawns shell or LOLBin child — AutoJack RCE outcome · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
AutoGen Studio browsing agent crosses loopback to MCP WebSocket (AutoJack) AIExploitation Low
Hunts the AutoJack confused-deputy step: an AutoGen agent's headless browser (Playwright/Chromium/node) or the python agent process opening a loopback WebSocket to AutoGen Studio's MCP control plane on 127.0.0.1:8081 carrying a base64 server_params payload. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact /api/mcp/ws endpoint and server_params query string that decode to StdioServerParams. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim endpoint /api/mcp/ws + server_params query string and port 8081 from the article's code blocks; cross-checked against The Hacker News and GBHackers which confirm the same WS surface and that the fix moved params to POST /api/mcp/ws/connect. Low confidence because EDR loopback telemetry is unreliable and the legit AutoGen Studio frontend also hits :8081. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/autojack-attack-lets-one-web-page.html • https://gbhackers.com/autojack-exploit-chain-hits-microsoft-autogen/
ATT&CKT1190 T1189
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate AutoGen Studio web UI (user's interactive Chrome/Edge) connecting to the local server on 127.0.0.1:8081
  • Developer manually testing an MCP server via the Studio UI on localhost
  • Another dev tool or service bound to port 8081 on the same host
  • Playwright/headless browser used for legitimate scraping that happens to hit a local service
  • Loopback health-check or hot-reload probes from the dev server itself
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has "server_params" == false and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","msedgewebview2.exe") and isnotempty(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "headless")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full RemoteUrl/SyslogMessage and base64-decode the server_params blob — a benign value decodes to a real MCP runtime (python/node/npx); a StdioServerParams with command=cmd.exe/powershell.exe/calc.exe/bash is malicious. Identify the initiating process and whether it is an agent's headless browser vs the user's interactive browser. 2) Contain: If the payload is a shell/LOLBin, isolate the host and kill the AutoGen Studio process; block the external page the agent rendered. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC 'AutoGen Studio python process spawning a shell or LOLBin' on the same DeviceId/time window to confirm whether the decoded command actually executed.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has "server_params" and RemoteUrl has "/api/mcp/ws")
    or (RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1") and RemotePort == 8081
        and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","node.exe","headless_shell.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","msedgewebview2.exe"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/api/mcp/ws" and SyslogMessage has "server_params"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AutoGen Studio MCP WebSocket loopback access carrying server_params (AutoJack)
id: 6f1c2a84-9b1d-4e3a-bb71-2d4a9c7e1f30
description: Detects a process opening a loopback connection to AutoGen Studio's MCP WebSocket on 127.0.0.1:8081, the AutoJack cross-localhost RCE primitive.

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=8081 RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\.0\.0\.1$/

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") All_Traffic.dest_port=8081 by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

AutoGen Studio (python) spawns shell or LOLBin child — AutoJack RCE outcome AIInstallation High
Hunts the execution result of AutoJack: the AutoGen Studio server (python/pythonw running autogenstudio) spawning an attacker-supplied process via stdio_client. Legitimate MCP servers are python/node/npx/uv; a shell, calc.exe, or LOLBin child is the verbatim PoC outcome (calc.exe, powershell.exe -enc, bash -c) and indicates the server_params command line was executed. Rationale: Uses the article's named PoC payloads (calc.exe, powershell.exe -enc, bash -c) executed under the developer's account by the autogenstudio python parent via stdio_client; the autogenstudio parent-cmdline anchor plus shell/LOLBin child keeps FPs low since legitimate MCP servers run as python/node/npx, not shells. Cross-checked against The Hacker News and GBHackers confirming command+args are spawned verbatim. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/autojack-attack-lets-one-web-page.html • https://gbhackers.com/autojack-exploit-chain-hits-microsoft-autogen/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately configuring a shell-wrapped MCP server in AutoGen Studio (e.g. cmd /c npx ...)
  • AutoGen agent code-execution tool legitimately invoking powershell/bash as part of an authorized workflow
  • CI or test harness launching autogenstudio that shells out during automated tests
  • Admin troubleshooting the Studio install from a python venv that spawns cmd.exe
  • Jupyter/IDE-launched python process unrelated to autogenstudio (excluded by the autogenstudio cmdline anchor)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npx","uvx","mcp-server","modelcontextprotocol","-m mcp") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child and InitiatingProcessCommandLine of the python parent — confirm the parent is the autogenstudio server and the child is not a legitimate MCP runtime wrapper (npx/uvx/node/mcp-server). Decode any base64 in the child cmdline. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, kill the python autogenstudio process and child, and capture the rendered page URL the agent visited. Pin AutoGen Studio to a build at or past upstream commit b047730 (or a PyPI release, which is unaffected). 3) Hunt: Pivot on the host/time window to UC 'browsing agent crosses loopback to MCP WebSocket', review subsequent network egress and persistence/registry writes by the child process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","calc.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","calc.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AutoGen Studio spawns shell or LOLBin child (AutoJack RCE)
id: a2e7d913-4c66-4f0b-9a18-7b3f5c10ad42
description: Detects the AutoGen Studio server (python running autogenstudio) spawning a shell, calc.exe, or LOLBin via stdio_client, the executed outcome of the AutoJack server_params injection.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/
  - https://gbhackers.com/autojack-exploit-chain-hits-microsoft-autogen/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1203
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: 'autogenstudio'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\calc.exe'
      - '\bash.exe'
      - '\wsl.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe OR *\Python.exe) @ParentCommandLine:*autogenstudio* @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\calc.exe OR *\bash.exe OR *\wsl.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\MSHTA.EXE OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe OR *\rundll32.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^pythonw?\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|calc|bash|wsl|mshta|wscript|cscript|regsvr32|rundll32|bitsadmin|certutil)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="python.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="pythonw.exe") Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio*" (Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="calc.exe" OR Processes.process_name="bash.exe" OR Processes.process_name="sh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="wsl.exe" OR Processes.process_name="mshta.exe" OR Processes.process_name="wscript.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cscript.exe" OR Processes.process_name="regsvr32.exe" OR Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" OR Processes.process_name="bitsadmin.exe" OR Processes.process_name="certutil.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="python.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="pythonw.exe") Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio*" (Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" OR Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="calc.exe" OR Processes.process_name="bash.exe" OR Processes.process_name="sh.exe" OR Processes.process_name="wsl.exe" OR Processes.process_name="mshta.exe" OR Processes.process_name="wscript.exe" OR Processes.process_name="cscript.exe" OR Processes.process_name="regsvr32.exe" OR Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" OR Processes.process_name="bitsadmin.exe" OR Processes.process_name="certutil.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:

       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

gemini-mcp-tool @file path-traversal / sensitive-file exfiltration via Gemini CLI AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Gemini CLI invocations (driven by the gemini-mcp-tool MCP server, CVE-2026-0755) whose command line carries an @file reference that escapes the working directory or targets sensitive files (@/etc/passwd, @~/.ssh/id_rsa, @../../secret). Article-specific because it keys on the Gemini CLI @file parser abuse used to read/exfiltrate arbitrary local files through the LLM channel. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact @file PoC strings (@/etc/passwd, @~/.ssh/id_rsa, @../../secret) scoped to a 'gemini' command line — the CVE-2026-0755 exfiltration sink. Cross-checked against the GitLab Advisory DB and Snyk entries which confirm the @file parser as the read/exfil vector. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/gemini-mcp-tool/CVE-2026-0755/ • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-GEMINIMCPTOOL-15091895 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-0755/
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately referencing a sibling project with @../other-repo/file.ts for cross-repo code analysis
  • Power user analyzing their own dotfiles, e.g. gemini -p 'review @~/.bashrc'
  • CI job pointing Gemini CLI at an absolute build-artifact path outside the checkout dir
  • Security researcher reproducing the CVE in an authorized test lab
  • Legitimate analysis of /var/log or /etc config files by an ops engineer using Gemini CLI
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)@\.\./[A-Za-z0-9._-]+/(src|lib|test|tests|docs)/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent (expect node.exe running the gemini-mcp-tool MCP server). Confirm the @file target is outside the project working directory and is sensitive (passwd, id_rsa, .env, cloud creds). Identify who/what supplied the prompt (MCP client, chat session, automated agent). 2) Contain: kill the MCP server process, upgrade gemini-mcp-tool to >=1.1.6, and rotate any credential file referenced (SSH keys, tokens) since the content was sent to the Gemini API. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to the Gemini API from this host around the event, search other hosts for the same gemini @traversal pattern, and check the MCP client logs for the originating untrusted prompt.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gemini"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)@(\.\.[\\/]|~[\\/]|/(etc|root|home|var|proc)/|[a-zA-Z]:\\)"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "gemini"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)@(\.\.[\\/]|~[\\/]|/(etc|root|home|var|proc)/|[a-zA-Z]:\\)"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

gemini-mcp-tool Windows cmd.exe metacharacter injection (node -> cmd.exe breakout) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-0755 Windows command-injection vector: the gemini-mcp-tool MCP server (node.exe) spawns cmd.exe to run the Gemini CLI, and unquoted prompt metacharacters break out of the gemini argument into arbitrary OS commands. Article-specific because it pivots on the node->cmd.exe chain carrying 'gemini' plus shell metacharacters (&, |, >, <, ^, `). Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact Windows injection mechanism — node-spawned cmd.exe running the Gemini CLI with unquoted metacharacters (the 'broken shell:false double-quote wrapping' the 1.1.6 fix removed). The node->cmd.exe->gemini chain is rare and the metacharacter requirement makes it alert-grade; corroborated by Penligent's execAsync sink analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4h5r-5jm8-jxjm • https://www.penligent.ai/hackinglabs/deep-analysis-of-gemini-mcp-tool-command-injection-cve-2026-0755-when-an-mcp-toolchain-hands-user-input-to-the-shell/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/gemini-mcp-tool/CVE-2026-0755/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1202
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate prompt that genuinely contains '&' or '|' inside quotes on a patched (>=1.1.6) host where quoting now contains it
  • Developer asking gemini about shell syntax, e.g. a prompt mentioning 'cmd & redirect'
  • Build wrapper that intentionally chains gemini with another command via cmd.exe (&&)
  • Local reproduction of the CVE in an authorized lab
  • A node-based task runner that pipes Gemini CLI output to a file with '>'
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)gemini[^\"]*[&|><^`]"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the cmd.exe ProcessCommandLine and isolate what follows the metacharacter after the gemini token — that is the injected command. Enumerate child processes of this cmd.exe (DeviceProcessEvents where InitiatingProcessId == this ProcessId) to see what actually executed (whoami, certutil, powershell, net). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node MCP server and any spawned children, and upgrade gemini-mcp-tool to >=1.1.6. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents from the host for download/exfil by the injected child, search for the same node->cmd->gemini+metacharacter pattern fleet-wide, and trace the originating untrusted prompt in the MCP client logs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gemini"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)gemini.*[&|><^`]"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "gemini"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)gemini.*[&|><^`]"
| where not(TargetUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, TargetUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "bf9672ec85283fdf002d83662f0b08b7", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

F5 Patches Two Critical NGINX Open Source Flaws Enabling Remote Code Execution

The Hacker News
2026-06-18 4 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

F5 has released security updates to address two critical security flaws in NGINX Open Source that could be exploited to achieve code execution on affected systems. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-42530 (CVSS v4 score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability in the ngx_http_v3_module that could be triggered by a remote unauthenticated attacker when NGINX Open Source is
