Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] NGINX hosts vulnerable to CVE-2026-42530 / CVE-2026-42055 (HTTP/3 UAF & HTTP/2 heap overflow) · [LLM] NGINX worker process crash-loop — memory-corruption exploitation of CVE-2026-42530/42055
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
NGINX hosts vulnerable to CVE-2026-42530 / CVE-2026-42055 (HTTP/3 UAF & HTTP/2 heap overflow) AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed host running an NGINX build affected by the two F5-patched RCE flaws so the SOC can prioritise internet-facing instances for patching/mitigation. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact CVE IDs F5 assigned; both are unauthenticated RCE-capable on systems where ASLR is disabled or bypassable. Rationale: Keys on the two exact CVE IDs (CVE-2026-42530, CVE-2026-42055) plus the NGINX software name from the advisory; CVE-mapped TVM inventory is deterministic and the internet-facing join elevates the highest-risk hosts F5 flagged as unauthenticated-RCE exploitable. Cross-checked against: • https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000161584 • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-78jw-ww3g-9wp7 • https://www.securityweek.com/f5-patches-critical-high-severity-nginx-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/f5-issues-out-of-band-patches-for-critical-nginx-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vuln scanner reports a version string for an NGINX module/wrapper (e.g. OpenResty, Tengine) that is not actually on the affected F5 build list
  • Host running a patched build (1.30.3 / 1.31.2 / R36 P6 / 37.0.2.1) still flagged by a stale scan before re-scan
  • NGINX present only as a transitive container layer that is never network-exposed
  • Backported distro package whose version string predates the fix but already carries the vendor patch
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !in ("1.30.3","1.31.2")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion against F5's fixed table (e.g. OSS fixed in 1.30.3/1.31.2, Plus R36 P6, NGINX Plus 37.0.2.1) and rule out backported/vendor-patched builds. 2) Contain: for unpatched internet-facing hosts apply F5's interim mitigations now — disable HTTP/3 (CVE-2026-42530); remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` or set `large_client_header_buffers` below 2MB (CVE-2026-42055) — then schedule the patch. 3) Hunt: on each affected host check NGINX error logs for worker-process crashes (pivot to the crash-loop UC) to detect any exploitation that already occurred.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055")
| where SoftwareName has "nginx"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing
| sort by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055")
| where SoftwareName has "nginx"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing
| sort by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Vulnerabilities.signature) as signature values(Vulnerabilities.severity) as severity from datamodel=Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort 0 dest
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Vulnerabilities.signature) as signature values(Vulnerabilities.severity) as severity from datamodel=Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort 0 dest
NGINX worker process crash-loop — memory-corruption exploitation of CVE-2026-42530/42055 AIExploitation Medium
Detects bursts of NGINX worker-process abnormal exits (SIGSEGV/SIGABRT) or rapid worker respawns, the observable symptom of both F5 RCE flaws — a HTTP/3 QPACK use-after-free and an oversized-HTTP/2-header heap overflow that crash the worker and, with ASLR bypass, yield code execution. Article-specific because both CVEs share this exact failure mode (worker restart) per F5's advisory. Rationale: Both CVEs' confirmed effect (per F5 + GitHub advisory) is an NGINX worker-process restart from heap/UAF corruption; SIGSEGV/SIGABRT crash-bursts and abnormal worker respawn rate are the highest-fidelity host signal of attempted exploitation when no payload IOCs exist. Cross-checked against: • https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000161584 • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-78jw-ww3g-9wp7 • https://securityaffairs.com/193842/security/f5-patches-critical-nginx-vulnerabilities-enabling-unauthenticated-code-execution.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OOM-killer terminating nginx workers under memory pressure (signal 9, not 11/6 — already excluded, but mixed log formats can leak)
  • Buggy third-party NGINX module crashing workers unrelated to these CVEs
  • Planned config reload / logrotate spawning fresh workers (SIGHUP, not a crash signal)
  • Blue/green deploy or container restart cycling many nginx workers in a short window
  • Disk-full or upstream-timeout storms causing repeated worker recycling
Suppression filter
| where SampleMessage !has "signal 9" and SampleMessage !has "gracefully shutting down" and SampleMessage !has "signal 1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the host's nginx error_log around the crash window; confirm SIGSEGV/SIGABRT (memory corruption) vs SIGKILL/OOM, and check the running NGINX version against the patched list plus whether HTTP/3 or HTTP/2-proxy+grpc_pass is enabled. 2) Contain: if unpatched and internet-facing, apply F5 mitigations immediately (disable HTTP/3; remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` or drop `large_client_header_buffers` below 2MB) and isolate/patch the host. 3) Hunt: correlate access/QUIC logs for the source IP sending oversized HTTP/2 headers (>2MB) or malformed HTTP/3 QPACK sessions just before each crash, and check for any non-nginx child process spawned by nginx (sign of successful RCE post-ASLR-bypass).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName == "nginx" and InitiatingProcessFileName == "nginx"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "worker process"
| summarize WorkerSpawns = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where WorkerSpawns >= 10   // healthy nginx rarely recycles workers; >=10 respawns / 10m = crash loop (baseline ~0)
| sort by LastSeen desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ProcessName == "nginx" or SyslogMessage has "nginx"
| where SyslogMessage has "exited on signal"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("signal 11","signal 6","SIGSEGV","SIGABRT","core dumped")
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CrashCount >= 3   // 3+ SIGSEGV/SIGABRT worker exits in 10m far exceeds normal (0)
| sort by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:nginx "exited on signal" ("signal 11" OR "signal 6" OR SIGSEGV OR SIGABRT)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/nginx$/i ParentBaseFileName=/nginx/i
| regex("worker process", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(as=WorkerSpawns))
| WorkerSpawns >= 10
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
`summariesonly`
| tstats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=nginx Processes.parent_process_name=nginx by Processes.dest Processes.process Processes.parent_process span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search process="*worker*"
| where count>=10
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort 0 - count
summariesonly=false
| tstats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=nginx Processes.parent_process_name=nginx by Processes.dest Processes.process Processes.parent_process span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search process="*worker*"
| where count>=10
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort 0 - count
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/

2026-06-18 2 use cases 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Crawl4AI: Unauthenticated RCE via Chromium launch-argument injection in browser_config.extra_args

ATT&CKT1190
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Chromium subprocess-launcher switch + --no-zygote co-occurrence (Crawl4AI extra_args RCE) · [LLM] Headless Chromium spawning shell/interpreter child (Crawl4AI injected-command exec)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Chromium subprocess-launcher switch + --no-zygote co-occurrence (Crawl4AI extra_args RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts a single Chromium/headless-shell process whose command line carries --no-zygote together with a subprocess-launcher override (--utility-cmd-prefix / --renderer-cmd-prefix / --gpu-launcher / --browser-subprocess-path). This tuple is the execution signature of GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44, where attacker-supplied browser_config.extra_args forces Chromium to fork/exec an arbitrary command. The combination is near-pathognomonic — legitimate Crawl4AI never sets a launcher-override prefix. Rationale: Uses the exact launcher-override switches named in the advisory (--utility-cmd-prefix/--renderer-cmd-prefix/--gpu-launcher/--browser-subprocess-path) gated on --no-zygote; per the Chromium zygote docs this combo is what forces a fresh fork/exec of the injected command, making it high-fidelity. Chromium switches are always lowercase canonical so no Datadog casing variants are needed. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44/ • https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/docs/linux/zygote.md
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer debugging Chromium under valgrind/gdb using --renderer-cmd-prefix on a workstation
  • CEF/Electron app that sets --no-zygote for stability but never sets a launcher prefix (won't match — requires both)
  • Automated browser-performance testing harness intentionally wrapping subprocesses
  • Crash-reproduction tooling that prefixes the GPU process launcher
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("valgrind","gdb","--enable-logging=stderr") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","make","ctest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and read the value after the launcher switch — that string IS the attacker command; capture the parent (Crawl4AI/uvicorn/python) and the runtime user. 2) Contain: kill the Chromium process tree, isolate/stop the Crawl4AI container, and rotate any secrets/tokens mounted into it (env, mounted files) since RCE ran as the runtime user. 3) Hunt: confirm the package is <=0.8.9, search for child processes the browser spawned (UC2), and review WAF/proxy logs for the POST /crawl* that delivered the payload (UC3).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "--no-zygote"
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "--utility-cmd-prefix"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--renderer-cmd-prefix"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--gpu-launcher"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--browser-subprocess-path"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--no-zygote"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--utility-cmd-prefix"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--renderer-cmd-prefix"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--gpu-launcher"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--browser-subprocess-path"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Chromium Subprocess-Launcher Switch With Zygote Disabled (Crawl4AI extra_args RCE)
id: 7b3e1c2a-4d5f-4a6b-8c9d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
description: Detects a Chromium/headless process launched with --no-zygote together with a subprocess-launcher override switch, the execution signature of GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44 argument-injection RCE in Crawl4AI.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44
  - https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/docs/linux/zygote.md
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_zygote:
    CommandLine|contains: '--no-zygote'
  selection_launcher:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--utility-cmd-prefix'
      - '--renderer-cmd-prefix'
      - '--gpu-launcher'
      - '--browser-subprocess-path'
  condition: selection_zygote and selection_launcher
falsepositives:
  - Bespoke browser-automation harnesses that deliberately set a launcher prefix for debugging
level: high
source:linux.auditd @process.command_line:*--no-zygote* AND @process.command_line:(*--utility-cmd-prefix* OR *--renderer-cmd-prefix* OR *--gpu-launcher* OR *--browser-subprocess-path*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("--no-zygote", field=CommandLine)
| CommandLine=/--(utility-cmd-prefix|renderer-cmd-prefix|gpu-launcher|browser-subprocess-path)/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*--no-zygote*" AND (Processes.process="*--utility-cmd-prefix*" OR Processes.process="*--renderer-cmd-prefix*" OR Processes.process="*--gpu-launcher*" OR Processes.process="*--browser-subprocess-path*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*--no-zygote*" AND (Processes.process="*--utility-cmd-prefix*" OR Processes.process="*--renderer-cmd-prefix*" OR Processes.process="*--gpu-launcher*" OR Processes.process="*--browser-subprocess-path*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Headless Chromium spawning shell/interpreter child (Crawl4AI injected-command exec) AIExploitation High
Hunts a browser process (chrome/chromium/headless_shell) that forks a shell, network tool or scripting interpreter as a direct child. In normal operation Chromium only spawns more Chromium/crashpad processes; a /bin/sh, curl, python or nc child is the post-exploitation result of the extra_args launcher-prefix injection executing the attacker command as the container runtime user. Rationale: Pivots on the parent→child relationship the advisory describes ('causing Chromium to fork/exec an attacker-controlled command'); in a Crawl4AI container the browser legitimately only spawns more browser/crashpad processes, so a shell/curl/python child is high-fidelity. Datadog left empty because the standard linux.auditd schema exposes no parent-process field to anchor the chain. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom crawler post-processing that legitimately pipes browser output through python/node
  • Container healthcheck scripts mis-parented under the browser during teardown
  • Debug builds invoking curl/wget from a browser test harness
  • Sandbox-disabled CI runs where the browser wrapper is a shell script
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","/usr/local/bin/entrypoint") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child ProcessCommandLine and any network destination it contacted; identify the runtime user and whether the child reached out-of-band (curl/wget/nc to an external IP). 2) Contain: terminate the child + Chromium tree, stop/quarantine the container, and block the egress destination at the firewall; rotate mounted secrets and tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (launcher-switch cmdline) on the same host/time, review FileWritten events by the child for dropped payloads, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for follow-on C2 from the runtime user.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome","chromium","chromium-browser","headless_shell","chrome-headless-shell","chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","netcat","perl","ruby","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome","chromium","chromium-browser","headless_shell","chrome-headless-shell")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","perl","ruby","node")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Crawl4AI RCE confirmation: cron/sshd/shell executes payload dropped by crawler within correlation window
Crawl4AI path-traversal: crawler Python process writes to RCE-enabling paths (cron.d, authorized_keys, shell rc, site-packages) AIInstallation High
Hunts the exploitation primitive of GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3: the crawl4ai download sink (HTTP Content-Disposition filename or Playwright suggested_filename) escaping the downloads directory and writing attacker-controlled bytes to one of the four RCE sinks the advisory names. A web-crawler Python process should never write to /etc/cron.d, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, shell rc files, or the Python import path, making this high-fidelity for the file-write-to-RCE escalation. Rationale: Uses the four RCE sinks the advisory explicitly names (/etc/cron.d/evil, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, shell rc-file, Python module on import path) keyed to a python initiating process, the only attacker-influenced behaviour this file-write-to-RCE bug produces. Cross-checked the GHSA, GitLab GLAD (CWE-22+CWE-59, fix 0.9.0) and VulnCheck's related crawl4ai Docker advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/crawl4ai-docker-api-local-file-inclusion-via-file-url-handling
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1098.004 T1546.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • pip/pip3 or poetry installing or upgrading a package writes legitimately into site-packages/dist-packages during a deploy of the crawler container
  • A maintenance/config-management Python script (Ansible/SaltStack module run via python) legitimately writing a cron job under /etc/cron.d
  • Developer running `python -m venv` or editable installs touching site-packages on a build host
  • Legitimate crawl4ai self-update writing its own package files
  • An ops automation Python tool rotating a service account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip","pip3","poetry","uv") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","setup.py","python -m venv")) and FolderPath has_any ("/site-packages/","/dist-packages/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and FolderPath/FileName — confirm the writer is the crawl4ai service (uvicorn/gunicorn/python crawler) and not pip/deploy tooling, and inspect the written file's content (cron line, SSH key, rc payload). Check the SHA256 and the source URL/Content-Disposition that triggered the download. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the crawler process, remove the dropped file, and rotate any exposed SSH keys/service creds; confirm crawl4ai is upgraded to >=0.9.0 and CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN auth is enabled. 3) Hunt: enumerate all files written by that python PID outside the downloads dir, review web/proxy logs for unauthenticated POSTs to the Docker /crawl endpoint with HTTPCrawlerConfig, and run UC2 to confirm whether cron/sshd executed the dropped payload.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "python" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "crawl4ai"
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/var/spool/cron","/site-packages/","/dist-packages/"))
    or FileName =~ "authorized_keys"
    or FileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_login")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "python" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "crawl4ai"
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/var/spool/cron","/site-packages/","/dist-packages/"))
    or TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys"
    or TargetFileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_login")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI RCE confirmation: cron/sshd/shell executes payload dropped by crawler within correlation window AIActions on Objectives Medium
Second-stage confirmation for GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3: after the crawl4ai Python process writes to /etc/cron.d or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, this correlates a subsequent process spawned by cron/crond/sshd (or a shell sourcing a modified rc) on the same host within 24h — evidence the arbitrary write actually escalated to code execution. Distinct pivot from UC1: process-execution telemetry joined to the file-write event, not the write alone. Rationale: Chains the UC1 drop (python writing /etc/cron.d or authorized_keys) to a cron/sshd-spawned execution on the same host inside 24h, confirming the advisory's stated escalation path (cron entry / authorized_keys -> RCE) actually fired rather than just the write attempt. Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ops automation that drops a cron job via a python config tool and the new cron job fires on schedule within the window
  • An admin adding their SSH key to authorized_keys via a python helper, then logging in via SSH (sshd-spawned shell)
  • Normal scheduled cron tasks running on a host where a python deploy touched /etc/cron.d for unrelated reasons

Suppression filter

Response runbook
1) Triage: open the joined record — confirm the cron/sshd child process maps to the file the crawler wrote (cron line content or the SSH session's source IP and key). Compare ExecFile/ProcessCommandLine against the dropped payload. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, disable the malicious cron entry and remove the unauthorized authorized_keys line, and terminate any active SSH sessions from unexpected source IPs. 3) Hunt: pivot on AccountName and source IP across DeviceLogonEvents for further SSH access, review outbound DeviceNetworkEvents from the spawned process for C2, and confirm crawl4ai is upgraded to >=0.9.0 across the fleet.

service-brother identity reaching admin/protected or mutating endpoints (post-bypass abuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces requests asserting auth-user: service-brother that target sensitive routes (/admin, /protected, /graphql, /internal) or use mutating methods (POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH) — i.e. the validateToken() bypass actually being used to act on protected resources rather than merely probed. Baseline legitimate service-brother destinations/methods and treat deviations as exploitation. Rationale: Combines the article's bypass marker (service-brother) with sensitive routes named in the fix (consumers: rest, graphql) and the example endpoint (/protected); mutating methods + 2xx on protected paths is the 'bypass was used' signal (reviewer #2/#4). The Splunk Web-datamodel half is the access-pattern net since CIM Web does not model request headers — confirm the header in WAF logs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@acastellon/auth/GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-GFJ5-979R-92PW
ATT&CKT1190 T1078 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate post-fix mTLS service-brother traffic that still carries the header while writing to admin/internal APIs
  • Internal automation/cron service accounts performing scheduled POST/PUT to /internal or /config
  • GraphQL introspection or schema-sync jobs hitting /graphql
  • Monitoring/synthetic probes that exercise /protected
  • Blue-team validation traffic after deploying the patch
Suppression filter
| where not(Message has_any ("client-cert","mtls","x-client-verify: SUCCESS")) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, confirm the request both asserts service-brother AND came from outside the service mesh; check the HTTP status — a 2xx on an admin/mutating route means the bypass succeeded. Diff the destination/method against the service-brother baseline. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate any secrets or data the route could expose, block the source, and enforce mTLS (TRUSTED_MTLS_SERVICES allowlist) so header-only identity is rejected. 3) Hunt: reconstruct the full session from that source across all routes, look for data exfil or further writes, and check downstream services that trusted the forwarded identity.

| where (Message has "service-brother" or RequestContext has "service-brother")
| where RequestMethod in~ ("POST","PUT","DELETE","PATCH") or RequestURL has_any ("/admin","/protected","/graphql","/internal","/users","/config")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable @acastellon/auth (<2.3.0) package present on host AIExploitation Medium
Inventory hunt for the affected npm package on disk — node_modules\@acastellon\auth\auth.js / package.json — which contains the spoofable validateToken() bypass below v2.3.0. Identifies servers running the vulnerable dependency so they can be patched before the header bypass is exploited; analyst confirms the exact version (2.2.0 vulnerable, fixed in 2.3.0+) from the package.json. Rationale: Targets the article's exact affected package and source file (auth.js) at the canonical npm scoped path; presence below v2.3.0 is the vulnerable surface for the bypass. This is the one detection expressible on endpoint/file telemetry since the header bypass itself is invisible to EDR. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@acastellon/auth/GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-GFJ5-979R-92PW
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer laptops or CI/build agents that pull the package into a test/scratch project
  • Hosts already upgraded to 2.3.0+ — identical file paths, only the package.json version differs (must be checked)
  • Security researcher reproducing the advisory in a lab
  • A transitive dependency vendoring the package that is not actually exposed on a network route
  • Container image build layers scanned at rest
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit, read node_modules/@acastellon/auth/package.json and confirm "version" < 2.3.0 (2.2.0 is the named vulnerable build); determine whether the host serves a public-facing route using validateToken(). 2) Contain: for internet-facing vulnerable hosts, deploy the edge WAF header-strip rule (auth-user, is-*) as an interim mitigation and prioritize upgrade to >=2.3.0 with mTLS service auth. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these hosts against the WAF header-bypass UCs to see if any received auth-user: service-brother traffic, and sweep the SBOM/lockfiles fleet-wide for the same dependency.

| where FileName in~ ("auth.js","package.json")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

netlicensing-mcp get_product called with path-traversal product_number (../token) AIExploitation High
Hunts MCP/application-log evidence of the netlicensing_get_product tool being invoked with a product_number containing path-traversal sequences (../, %2e%2e, %2f, %5c). This is the raw attacker input for GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8, captured before httpx normalizes /product/../token into /token. Rationale: Uses the exact MCP tool name (netlicensing_get_product) plus the article's documented traversal payloads (../token and the encoded variants %2e%2e/%2f/%5c the remediation adds regression tests for). A Product-fetch tool receiving path separators in its identifier argument has no legitimate use. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: the payload is an in-process MCP tool argument, not a Windows process command line or AWS API call. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://netlicensing.io/wiki/restful-api • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8

| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("regression-test", "pytest", "VULN-001", "scanner"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full log line — confirm the tool is netlicensing_get_product and the product_number literally contains ../ , %2e%2e, %2f or %5c. Identify the MCP client identity / API key that made the call. 2) CONTAIN: If product is < 0.1.8, treat as confirmed exploit — rotate the NetLicensing API key the MCP server holds, and any APIKEY tokens (especially ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN) that could have been disclosed; upgrade to >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Search the same source for other tool calls from this client and for get_product responses containing tokenType/APIKEY (UC3) to confirm whether a key was actually returned.

NetLicensing REST request URL containing both /product/ and traversal-to-token (wire signature) AIExploitation High
Hunts forward-proxy / SWG logs for a single request to go.netlicensing.io (or backup netlicensing.labs64.com) whose URL contains the /product/ segment together with /token or an encoded traversal sequence — the on-the-wire artefact when the percent-encoded GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 payload survives httpx normalization. Legitimate traffic hits /product OR /token, never both in one URL. Rationale: Anchors on the confirmed REST base host go.netlicensing.io (+backup netlicensing.labs64.com) and the structural impossibility of a legitimate URL containing both /product/ and a token/traversal segment. Targets the encoded variants (%2e%2e/%2f/%5c) that survive WHATWG normalization to the wire. Datadog empty: no web-proxy source in this tenant's source list; Defender/Falcon empty: no HTTP path visibility inside HTTPS to a SaaS endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://netlicensing.io/wiki/restful-api
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic

  • A proxy that pre-normalizes URLs and rewrites %2e%2e (would suppress, not false-positive)
  • Manual cURL testing by an engineer reproducing the advisory
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the proxy log shows a single request to go.netlicensing.io with /product/ + token/traversal in the URL; identify the SourceIP (the MCP server host) and any authenticated SourceUserName. 2) CONTAIN: Block/inspect the source if unauthorized; rotate the NetLicensing API key the MCP server uses and any potentially-exposed APIKEY tokens; ensure the package is upgraded to >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Pivot to MCP/app logs (UC1) for the originating get_product call and to UC4 for bare /token hits from the same host that the literal ../ form would have produced.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any ("go.netlicensing.io","netlicensing.labs64.com")
| where RequestURL contains "/product/"
| where RequestURL contains "/token" or RequestURL contains "%2e%2e" or RequestURL contains "%2f" or RequestURL contains "%5c" or RequestURL contains "/../"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

netlicensing-mcp get_product response leaking APIKEY/token fields (redaction bypass) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts MCP/application logs for a netlicensing_get_product (Product-typed) tool call whose output contains token-specific fields — tokenType APIKEY, ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN, or a console_url under /#/tokens/. Per GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 these are exactly the fields redact_token_read() would mask; a Product tool returning them is direct evidence the traversal reached /token and leaked a plaintext key. Rationale: Pairs the Product tool name with the exact token-leak markers from the advisory's PoC output (tokenType=APIKEY, role ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN, console_url https://ui.netlicensing.io/#/tokens/<key>). The legitimate token tools (get_token/list_tokens) may emit these too, but a PRODUCT tool emitting them is unambiguous bypass evidence. Hunting tier because it depends on the deployment logging tool responses. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: app-layer response content unavailable to those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8
ATT&CKT1212 T1552
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Verbose debug logging that echoes a legitimate get_token response near a get_product log line (correlation artefact)
  • Replay of the published PoC output in a test/log-sample dataset
  • A custom downstream tool that legitimately enriches product data with token metadata (rare; should be validated)
  • Log aggregation that interleaves get_product and get_token messages making string co-occurrence appear in one record
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the record is a get_product RESPONSE (not a get_token call) carrying a real (unmasked) APIKEY number/console_url. Note the MCP client identity and the leaked token's role. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately revoke/rotate the disclosed APIKEY token — if ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN, treat the entire NetLicensing account as compromised (full read/write/delete) and rotate the account owner credential; upgrade to >=0.1.8. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all get_product calls from this client (UC1) to scope which keys were exfiltrated, and review NetLicensing audit/console activity for use of the leaked admin token.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "netlicensing_get_product"
| where SyslogMessage has "ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN" or (SyslogMessage has "tokenType" and SyslogMessage has "APIKEY") or SyslogMessage contains "/#/tokens/"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog netlicensing_get_product AND ("ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN" OR "tokenType" OR "/#/tokens/")
APPLICATION
index=* "netlicensing_get_product" ("ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN" OR "tokenType" OR "/#/tokens/")
| table _time host source _raw
| sort - _time
First-seen access to NetLicensing /token REST endpoint from MCP egress source AIActions on Objectives Medium
Behavioral baseline over proxy logs: flags a source host issuing GET /core/v2/rest/token to go.netlicensing.io when that source has no prior history of token-endpoint access in the baseline window. This covers the GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 case where the literal ../token payload is normalized by httpx to a bare /token request that carries no traversal artefact on the wire. Rationale: Catches the literal ../token variant that UC2 misses (httpx collapses /product/../token to a bare /token GET). Because the dedicated token tools also legitimately hit /token, this relies on a 14-day per-source baseline so only newly-token-active sources surface — Medium confidence by design. Anchored on the confirmed REST path /core/v2/rest/token. Datadog empty (no proxy source in tenant list); Defender/Falcon empty (no HTTPS path visibility). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/netlicensing-mcp/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8/ • https://netlicensing.io/wiki/restful-api

  • New MCP server instance deployed in the baseline-free window
  • Proxy NAT change re-mapping an existing token-user to a new SourceIP

| where SourceIP !in ("")  // populate with confirmed-benign MCP/token-tool egress IPs after first triage to suppress benign new-adopter sources

1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the new source's /token access correlates with a get_product call in MCP/app logs (UC1/UC3). Vulnerable googleapis/mcp-toolbox (< 1.4.0) — CVE-2026-11718 opaque-token auth bypass present AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces any managed host whose vulnerability feed reports CVE-2026-11717 / CVE-2026-11718 against the googleapis/mcp-toolbox Go package. This hunts the specific auth-bypass advisory (validateOpaqueToken accepting introspection responses that omit the mandatory RFC 7662 "active" field), not a generic missing-patch query — it anchors on the exact CVE IDs and the mcp-toolbox software name. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two concrete identifiers (CVE-2026-11717/11718) and the affected package name github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox; deterministic CVE-feed match, so FP is limited to stale-inventory rather than behavioural noise. Cross-checked the GHSA against CyberPress, CyberSecurityNews and the upstream GitHub issue #3076 which confirm fix version 1.4.0 and CVSS 4.0 9.3. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcpr-6g7x-p44r • https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox/issues/3076 • https://cyberpress.org/mcp-toolbox-vulnerability-exposed/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/mcp-toolbox-vulnerability/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-11718
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already upgraded to 1.4.0+ but the TVM/scanner snapshot is stale and a re-scan is still pending
  • CVE feed maps the Go module under a SoftwareName that doesn't contain 'toolbox' (vendor naming drift), so a real device is missed rather than false-positive
  • Isolated dev/CI box intentionally pinned to an old version inside a non-routable network
  • Vendored / build-artifact copy of the module flagged as 'installed' though no toolbox service is actually listening
  • Container image scanned by the feed though the image is ephemeral and already destroyed
Suppression filter
| join kind=inner (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | where SoftwareName has_any ("mcp-toolbox","toolbox") | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId | extend CleanVer = trim_start(@"[vV]", SoftwareVersion) | where CleanVer matches regex @"^\d+(\.\d+)+" | where parse_version(CleanVer) < parse_version("1.4.0")) on DeviceId
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each dest/DeviceName, confirm a mcp-toolbox process is actually listening (default port 5000) and note whether it's internet-facing; pull SoftwareVersion to verify it is genuinely < 1.4.0 and not a stale record. 2) CONTAIN: Patch to >= 1.4.0 (the fixed release); if patching is delayed, restrict the toolbox's network exposure to trusted clients and verify the configured OAuth introspection endpoint is a trusted, RFC 7662-compliant server that always returns the 'active' field. 3) HUNT: Review toolbox/auth access logs for tool invocations that succeeded against an introspection response lacking 'active', and check for the sibling advisories on the same hosts (CVE-2026-9739 SSE DNS-rebinding, and the issuer-field bypass variant).

| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Internet-facing host running vulnerable mcp-toolbox (< 1.4.0) — exposed auth-bypass surface AIExploitation Medium
Prioritises CVE-2026-11718 exposure by cross-referencing the mcp-toolbox software inventory (version < 1.4.0, the fixed release) against assets flagged internet-facing. Targets the externally reachable instances where an attacker-influenced or non-compliant introspection endpoint could trigger the validateOpaqueToken bypass — a different pivot (inventory + exposure join) than the raw CVE-feed match. Rationale: Uses the article's fixed-version boundary (1.4.0) for an explicit parse_version comparison and the package name, then joins DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing to rank externally exposed instances — the highest-risk targets for a remote token-validation bypass (T1190). Sentinel lacks the DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory table, so the Sentinel variant expresses the same intent via the CVE feed joined to internet-facing assets. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcpr-6g7x-p44r • https://cyberpress.org/mcp-toolbox-vulnerability-exposed/ • https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox/issues/3076
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SoftwareVersion carries a pre-release/build suffix (e.g. '1.4.0-rc1') that passes the regex but is functionally patched
  • IsInternetFacing flag is stale — host has since been moved behind a firewall or load balancer
  • mcp-toolbox present only as a transitive SDK/library, not the exposed listening server
  • Reverse proxy / WAF fronts the toolbox so the flagged host is exposed but the toolbox port is not actually reachable
  • Inventory shows old version string cached after an in-place binary swap to 1.4.0
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.4." and SoftwareVersion !startswith "v1.4."
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the toolbox listener is reachable from the public IP (probe the configured port, default 5000) and that SoftwareVersion is genuinely < 1.4.0; validate the OAuth introspection endpoint it trusts is RFC 7662-compliant and always emits 'active'. 2) CONTAIN: Take the external exposure offline or front it with auth-enforcing proxy; upgrade to >= 1.4.0. 3) HUNT: Pull the toolbox/auth logs for the exposure window and look for tool-invocation successes tied to introspection responses missing 'active', plus the related SSE DNS-rebinding (CVE-2026-9739) and issuer-omission bypass on the same internet-facing fleet.

| where SoftwareName has_any ("mcp-toolbox", "toolbox") and SoftwareVendor has "google"
| extend CleanVer = trim_start(@"[vV]", SoftwareVersion)
| where CleanVer matches regex @"^\d+(\.\d+)+"
| where parse_version(CleanVer) < parse_version("1.4.0")
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| where IsInternetFacing == true

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kirby Panel install surface accessed on a live site (CVE-2026-54003)

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Kirby Panel install surface accessed on a live site (CVE-2026-54003) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts any HTTP request to the Kirby Panel installation routes (/panel/installation or /api/system/install) on a production site. An already-initialised Kirby install never legitimately serves these routes, so traffic here on a live site indicates external-initialization probing or exploitation of CVE-2026-54003 via the spoofable Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP headers. Rationale: Uses the exact Kirby install routes /panel/installation and /api/system/install named in the advisory and confirmed in Kirby docs; on a live site any non-404/403 hit is anomalous. Client-IP filtering is deliberately omitted because behind a reverse proxy the logged cIP is the proxy, not the attacker (the spoofed IP lives in the Forwarded/X-Real-IP header). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-whxw-24jc-cwmv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/getkirby/cms/CVE-2026-54003/ • https://github.com/getkirby/kirby/releases/tag/5.4.4
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet background scanners probing common CMS/admin paths like /panel
  • Legitimate first-time deployment of a brand-new Kirby site within the maintenance window
  • Authorized vulnerability scanning or pentest engagement against the site
  • Synthetic uptime/availability monitors crawling Panel routes
  • Staging/dev Kirby instance shipping access logs into the same workspace
Suppression filter
| where toint(scStatus) !in (404, 403)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull all install-route hits; check the response code and whether this host is a brand-new deploy (no admin yet) versus an established site. Cross-reference proxy logs for the Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP header and the true client IP. 2) Contain: If the site was already live, treat as compromise — set 'api'=>false or take Panel offline, and update Kirby to 4.9.4/5.4.4. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC 'admin account created' to see if a POST succeeded, then review Panel logins, new users, and uploaded templates/plugins for webshells.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/panel/installation" or csUriStem has "/api/system/install"
| where toint(scStatus) !in (404, 403)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kirby remote first-admin creation via unauthenticated install POST (CVE-2026-54003) AIInstallation High
Alerts on a successful POST to the Kirby install API (/api/system/install or /panel/installation) returning a 2xx status. On a publicly reachable Kirby site this means the first admin account was created without authentication by abusing the Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP isLocal bypass — the actual exploitation and persistence step of CVE-2026-54003. Rationale: Keys on the exact install API route plus method=POST and a 2xx response — a combination that on an already-deployed Kirby site means an admin was actually created without auth, which is the precise impact the advisory describes. Status filter separates successful exploitation from harmless scanner probes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-whxw-24jc-cwmv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/getkirby/cms/CVE-2026-54003/ • https://github.com/getkirby/kirby/releases/tag/5.4.4
ATT&CKT1190 T1136
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional first-time install by an admin with panel.install enabled during a deploy window
  • DevOps automation that provisions the first admin via the install endpoint
  • Fresh staging/dev deploy that legitimately has no users yet
  • A redeploy that wiped the accounts/ directory and is being re-initialised on purpose
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm scStatus 2xx on the POST and verify the site was already live (had an admin) rather than a planned new deploy; capture cIP and the true client IP from proxy Forwarded/X-Real-IP headers. 2) Contain: Immediately delete the attacker-created admin account, invalidate all Panel sessions, set 'api'=>false or take the Panel offline, and upgrade to Kirby 4.9.4/5.4.4. 3) Hunt: Review all Panel logins and actions from the new account, content/blueprint/template changes, additional user creations, and any uploaded PHP for webshells; pivot on the source IP across other sites.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/api/system/install" or csUriStem has "/panel/installation"
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where toint(scStatus) in (200, 201)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Details Windows Clipper Malware Campaign Using USB LNK Worm and Tor-Based C2

The Hacker News
2026-06-18 9 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has disclosed details of a Windows-based cryptocurrency clipper campaign codenamed CryptoBandits that has targeted users since February 2026 with clipboard-intercepting malware with self-spreading capabilities and using the Tor anonymity network to hide communication. "The clipper in this campaign relies on Windows Script Host and ActiveX-driven logic to launch a bundled Tor proxy and

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] USB LNK worm cloning documents into shortcuts - CryptoBandits propagation
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Windows Script Host (wscript/cscript) spawning renamed Tor proxy, curl or shell - CryptoBandits clipper · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Scheduled task persistence created by Windows Script Host - CryptoBandits worm/clipper · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Renamed portable Tor client (ugate.exe / Tor metadata masquerade) - CryptoBandits SOCKS5 backdoor · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PowerShell screen capture staged for Tor exfiltration - CryptoBandits clipper · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Windows Script Host (wscript/cscript) spawning renamed Tor proxy, curl or shell - CryptoBandits clipper AIExploitation High
Hunts the CryptoBandits clipper's core execution behaviour: a WScript/CScript host launching the bundled Tor client (ugate.exe), curl, cmd or PowerShell. Microsoft explicitly recommends behavioural detection of script engines spawning these binaries for this campaign. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated execution chain (WScript/ActiveX launching a bundled Tor proxy + curl/cmd/PowerShell) and the corroborated Tor binary name ugate.exe; the ProcessVersionInfoProductName has 'Tor' clause catches the binary even if renamed away from ugate.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://www.securityweek.com/cryptobandits-malware-doubles-as-a-backdoor-abuses-tor/ • https://cyberpress.org/tor-proxy-malware-control/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business VBScript/JScript installers that shell out to cmd.exe for setup tasks
  • Admin logon scripts (wscript) that call curl.exe to fetch config or PowerShell for inventory
  • Software deployment frameworks (SCCM/Intune) that wrap script-host bootstrappers around rundll32
  • Privileged orchestration tooling running scheduled VBScripts that spawn powershell.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Microsoft\", @"\CCM\", @"\Intune") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and the wscript/cscript ParentCmd; confirm the script path and whether the child is ugate.exe / a binary carrying Tor version metadata. Check the script's origin folder (removable drive or %TEMP%/%APPDATA%). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the wscript/cscript and child process tree, and block the script + ugate.exe hashes. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for localhost:9050 connections, schtasks /create by script host, mass .lnk creation on drives, and PowerShell screen-capture - the other CryptoBandits stages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("ugate.exe","tor.exe","curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Tor"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildProduct = ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\ugate.exe", @"\tor.exe", @"\curl.exe", @"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\mshta.exe", @"\rundll32.exe", @"\regsvr32.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Renamed portable Tor client (ugate.exe / Tor metadata masquerade) - CryptoBandits SOCKS5 backdoor AICommand & Control High
Identifies the CryptoBandits portable Tor client deployed as ugate.exe, or any binary carrying The Tor Project's PE version metadata while renamed away from tor.exe. This Tor instance opens a local SOCKS5 proxy on 127.0.0.1:9050 to reach the hidden-service C2. Rationale: Uses the corroborated renamed-Tor IOC ugate.exe plus a masquerade clause (Tor PE metadata on a non-tor.exe image) so the rule survives a rename; the SOCKS5-on-9050 behaviour described in the article is what this binary stands up. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberpress.org/tor-proxy-malware-control/ • https://www.securityweek.com/cryptobandits-malware-doubles-as-a-backdoor-abuses-tor/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1036.005 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tor Browser Bundle installs where the user legitimately runs tor.exe (excluded), but a portable copy renamed by a power user could trip the metadata clause
  • Privacy/anonymity research tooling that bundles a renamed Tor binary
  • Pentest/red-team toolkits shipping Tor under a non-standard name during sanctioned engagements
  • Security products that embed a Tor stub with their own product metadata
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","explorer.exe","cmd.exe") or FileName =~ "ugate.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the image's PE metadata (CompanyName 'The Tor Project', OriginalFileName tor.exe) versus its on-disk name; capture SHA256 and the launching parent (expect wscript/cscript). 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate ugate.exe, block the hash, and capture netstat for a 127.0.0.1:9050 listener. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent script, scheduled tasks created by script host, and clipboard/screenshot activity to scope full CryptoBandits infection.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "ugate.exe"
    or ((ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Tor" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "tor.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Tor") and FileName !in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          OriginalFileName = ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName,
          Company = ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\ugate.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Renamed Portable Tor Client - CryptoBandits ugate.exe SOCKS5 Backdoor

Scheduled task persistence created by Windows Script Host - CryptoBandits worm/clipper AIInstallation High
Detects the CryptoBandits worm registering scheduled-task persistence for both the worm and the clipper module by having wscript.exe/cscript.exe invoke schtasks.exe /create. Script-host-created scheduled tasks are rare in benign environments. Rationale: Article states the worm deploys scheduled tasks for both the worm and the stealer; pairing schtasks /create with a script-host parent is high-fidelity because benign scheduled tasks are almost never created by wscript/cscript interactively. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://cyberinsider.com/microsoft-warns-of-usb-worm-like-malware-using-tor-for-stealth/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy application setup VBScripts that register a maintenance scheduled task on first run
  • Admin/MDM logon scripts that create user-level scheduled tasks via schtasks
  • Software updaters bootstrapped from a .vbs wrapper that self-schedule recurring checks
  • Helpdesk remediation scripts run interactively that create a one-off cleanup task
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Microsoft\", "updater") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full schtasks /create command line - capture /tn task name, /tr action (expect it to point at wscript running the worm/clipper script or ugate.exe), and the parent script path. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task (schtasks /delete /tn <name>), isolate the host, and kill the script-host tree. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks on the host and across the fleet whose action references wscript/cscript or ugate.exe; check for the paired worm + clipper tasks the campaign installs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          TaskCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Created by Windows Script Host (CryptoBandits Persistence)

PowerShell screen capture staged for Tor exfiltration - CryptoBandits clipper AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the CryptoBandits screenshot-exfiltration stage: PowerShell using GDI/Drawing screen-capture APIs (CopyFromScreen, Drawing.Bitmap, PrimaryScreen, BitBlt). Microsoft specifically flagged PowerShell-based screen capture as a behavioural indicator for this campaign. Rationale: Targets the article's screenshot-exfiltration capability via the specific .NET screen-capture API tokens Microsoft called out for PowerShell-based screen capture; these strings rarely appear in benign command lines. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/microsoft-details-windows-clipper.html
ATT&CKT1113 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT remote-support / monitoring scripts that screenshot a user session for diagnostics
  • Screen-recording or kiosk-monitoring agents implemented in PowerShell
  • QA/test-automation harnesses capturing screenshots of the desktop
  • DLP or insider-risk tooling that periodically captures screen state
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","monitoringhost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full PowerShell command line - confirm it builds a Bitmap from PrimaryScreen and where the image is saved/sent; check the parent (wscript/cscript points to CryptoBandits). 2) Contain: if malicious, isolate the host, kill the PowerShell + script-host tree, and block ugate.exe / the script hashes. 3) Hunt: correlate with ugate.exe execution and 127.0.0.1:9050 SOCKS activity on the same host to confirm screenshots are leaving via Tor; sweep the fleet for the same API token usage from a script-host parent.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("CopyFromScreen","Drawing.Bitmap","FromImage","PrimaryScreen","BitBlt")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("CopyFromScreen","Drawing.Bitmap","FromImage","PrimaryScreen","BitBlt")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell Screen Capture API Usage (CryptoBandits Exfiltration)

USB LNK worm cloning documents into shortcuts - CryptoBandits propagation AIDelivery Medium
Detects the CryptoBandits worm component cloning harvested DOC/XLSX/PDF files into same-named .lnk shortcuts: a script host (wscript/cscript) creating multiple .lnk files in a short span. The original documents are hidden so the user clicks the malicious shortcut instead. Rationale: Encodes the article's propagation mechanic - the worm scans the USB drive for DOC/XLSX/PDF, hides them, and creates same-named .lnk files pointing to the worm; a script-host creating 3+ shortcuts at once is a tight behavioural signature of that cloning loop. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/ • https://cyberinsider.com/microsoft-warns-of-usb-worm-like-malware-using-tor-for-stealth/
ATT&CKT1091 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Logon or deployment VBScripts that drop multiple Start Menu / Desktop shortcuts during app install
  • User profile setup scripts that recreate pinned shortcuts at first sign-in
  • Backup/sync tooling wrapped in a script host that rebuilds .lnk references
  • Software packaging tools generating shortcut sets via cscript
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install", "setup", "deploy", @"\Start Menu\") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the created .lnk targets - CryptoBandits shortcuts point back to wscript/cscript running the worm script and their names mirror real DOC/XLSX/PDF files now hidden in the same folder. Check the folder for hidden originals. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the script-host tree, quarantine the worm script and .lnk files, and scan/eject any connected removable media. 3) Hunt: enumerate other drives/hosts that mounted the same USB, and look for the paired scheduled-task persistence and ugate.exe execution to confirm full infection.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize LnkCount = dcount(FileName), LnkFiles = make_set(FileName, 20),
            Folders = make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where LnkCount >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".lnk"
| summarize LnkCount = dcount(TargetFileName), Files = make_set(TargetFileName, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where LnkCount >= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe) @TargetFilename:(*.lnk OR *.LNK)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i TargetFileName=/\.lnk$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=LnkCount))
| LnkCount >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Filesystem.file_name) as lnk_count values(Filesystem.file_name) as lnk_files min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" AND (Filesystem.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND Filesystem.action="created" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where lnk_count >= 3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Filesystem.file_name) as lnk_count values(Filesystem.file_name) as lnk_files min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" AND (Filesystem.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND Filesystem.action="created" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where lnk_count >= 3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Internet-facing PraisonAI platform booting on default JWT secret (CVE-2026-47410) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts hosts running praisonai-platform's documented entry point bound to 0.0.0.0 (python -m praisonai_platform / uvicorn praisonai_platform.api.app). Because PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET/PLATFORM_ENV are set nowhere in the package, any such exposed instance signs session JWTs with the public literal 'dev-secret-change-me' and is pre-auth forgeable. Surfaces the vulnerable deployment so an analyst can confirm the env vars are actually set. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact documented entry point strings (praisonai_platform, uvicorn praisonai_platform.api.app, --host 0.0.0.0) — the article states neither PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET nor PLATFORM_ENV is set anywhere in the package, so any matching internet-bound process is the vulnerable default state. Cross-checked against GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 and the GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/staging instance where PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET is exported in the shell or systemd unit (not visible on cmdline) so the deployment is actually safe
  • Container CI smoke-test that boots the server transiently then tears down
  • Reverse-proxy fronted deployment where 0.0.0.0 binding is intentional and the secret is set via Docker secret/env-file
  • Security team running the package in a lab to reproduce the advisory
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the surfaced host, check the running process environment for PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET (e.g. `cat /proc/<pid>/environ | tr '\0' '\n' | grep PLATFORM_`) — if absent or equal to 'dev-secret-change-me', the instance is forgeable. 2) CONTAIN: Pull the service off the public interface (firewall the port / bind to localhost), export a strong random PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET and PLATFORM_ENV=production, restart, and invalidate all outstanding sessions (every issued JWT was signed with the public key). 3) HUNT: Review the web/proxy logs for this service for the workspace-member enumeration and owner-gated DELETE activity (see companion UCs) to determine if forgery was already exercised.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "praisonai_platform"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("uvicorn", "-m praisonai_platform", "praisonai_platform.api.app")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai_platform"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("uvicorn", "-m praisonai_platform", "praisonai_platform.api.app")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
