PraisonAI workspace/member destruction via owner-gated routes (forged-JWT takeover impact) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects successful DELETE requests against praisonai-platform's owner-gated routes — DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} (full workspace + contained resources) and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id} (legitimate-member eviction). With the auth bypass these are reachable by an attacker holding only a forged owner JWT, yielding irrecoverable lock-out (A:H). Rationale: Pivots on the advisory's exact owner-gated route names (DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}) called out as the resource-destruction / lock-out endpoints. Web-tier only because forgery and verification happen in-process with no endpoint signal. Cross-checked against the GitHub and GitLab advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/
ATT&CKT1485 T1531 T1606
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine workspace owner deleting a workspace they no longer need
  • Admin offboarding a departed employee via DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}
  • Automated cleanup job pruning stale demo/trial workspaces
  • QA teardown of test workspaces in a non-prod tenant
Suppression filter
| where CIp !in ("<known-admin-egress-ips>")  // remove this line and substitute your real admin egress CIDRs via an ip range watchlist; alternatively join to an allowlist of legitimate owner UPNs on CsUsername
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the source IP, User-Agent and any captured CsUsername for the DELETE; correlate the same source against the member-enumeration UC and the host-exposure UC — a delete preceded by a GET /{workspace_id}/members burst from the same IP strongly indicates forged-token takeover rather than a real owner. 2) CONTAIN: If forgery is suspected, rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET immediately (this invalidates every forged and legitimate token), block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, and restore the deleted workspace/members from backup. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all DELETE and owner-gated mutation calls (member role changes, resource deletes) from the same IP/UA across every workspace to scope the blast radius.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "DELETE"
| where CsUriStem matches regex @"(?i)^/workspaces/[^/]+/?$"
     or CsUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/[^/]+/members/[^/]+/?$"
| where ScStatus between (200 .. 299)
| project TimeGenerated, CIp, CsUsername, CsHost, CsMethod, CsUriStem, ScStatus, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI workspace member enumeration harvesting owner user_ids (pre-takeover recon) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single source listing members across many workspaces via GET /{workspace_id}/members. The advisory states the response (List[MemberResponse], each carrying user_id and role) is how an attacker learns a workspace owner's uuid4 id — the one extra fact needed to forge an owner token and pivot from anonymous bypass to targeted owner takeover. Rationale: Pivots on the advisory's named recon primitive: GET /{workspace_id}/members returns each member's user_id and role to any member, which is exactly how an attacker obtains an owner's otherwise-unguessable uuid4 id. Fan-out across many workspaces from one source is the high-fidelity discriminator versus a real owner viewing their own one workspace. Threshold-based so no Sigma. Cross-checked against GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai-platform/CVE-2026-47410/
ATT&CKT1087 T1606
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/support console legitimately iterating member lists across many workspaces
  • Billing or analytics service account that periodically reads membership for all workspaces
  • Internal vulnerability scanner crawling the API surface
  • A power user who genuinely owns/belongs to many workspaces and opens each members page in a session
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "PraisonAI-Admin" and CsUsername !in ("svc-billing", "svc-analytics")  // suppress known internal service accounts/tools that legitimately sweep member lists
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the source IP/UA and whether it maps to a known service account or admin tool; an unfamiliar IP reading 5+ workspaces' member lists in minutes is the harvesting signal. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source at the proxy/WAF and, if the host-exposure UC confirms the instance runs on the default secret, rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET and set PLATFORM_ENV=production to kill the forgery primitive before owner-id harvesting can be weaponised. 3) HUNT: Pivot the same source forward in time to any owner-gated mutation (DELETE workspace/member, role change) — see the destruction UC — to confirm whether harvested ids were used to forge owner tokens.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CsMethod == "GET"
| where CsUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/[^/]+/members/?$"
| where ScStatus between (200 .. 299)
| summarize WorkspacesEnumerated = dcount(CsUriStem), SampleRoutes = make_set(CsUriStem, 10), TotalReqs = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsUsername, UserAgent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where WorkspacesEnumerated >= 5   // one source reading the member list of 5+ distinct workspaces in 10 min = owner-id harvesting, not normal owner browsing
| order by WorkspacesEnumerated desc

PraisonAI multiedit arbitrary write to SSH/shell/cloud-cred files by python process AIInstallation High
Hunts a PraisonAI agent (python) abusing the unvalidated `multiedit` filepath parameter to overwrite security-sensitive files outside the workspace — ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.bashrc/.profile, ~/.aws/credentials, .env. This is the write primitive of GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 used for persistence/privilege escalation, and is article-specific because it ties the named tool's host process to writes against the exact protected paths the advisory calls out. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact write-target paths (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.bashrc, ~/.aws/credentials, .env) bound to the python host process of the named multiedit tool; high-fidelity because authorized_keys/.bashrc writes by an interpreter are rare. Cross-checked against the GitHub Advisory and the broader PraisonAI path-traversal advisory cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4171215/praisonai-vulnerability-gets-scanned-within-4-hours-of-disclosure.html
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1546.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Python application/deployment script writing its own project-local .env file inside the app workspace
  • Configuration-management tooling written in Python (Ansible local modules, custom provisioning) updating ~/.bashrc or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
  • Developer Jupyter/python session legitimately editing dotfiles during environment setup
  • Cloud SDK helper writing ~/.aws/credentials during an authorized `aws configure`-style automation
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ ".env" and FolderPath has_any ("/site-packages/","/node_modules/","/.venv/","/venv/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain — confirm the writer is a PraisonAI agent/CLI (look for 'praisonai'/'multiedit') and whether the target path is outside the agent's intended workspace. Capture the before/after file contents (esp. authorized_keys new keys, .bashrc appended commands). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the agent process, revoke/rotate any keys or cloud credentials in the touched files, and remove attacker-added authorized_keys entries. 3) Hunt: pin praisonai version (must be >= 4.6.61); search the same host and peer agents for multiedit reads of secrets (see credential-read UC), unexpected outbound C2 from python, and downstream use of stolen ~/.aws/credentials in cloud logs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "python" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","multiedit")
| where (FileName =~ "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh/")
     or FileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_aliases")
     or (FileName =~ "credentials" and FolderPath has "/.aws/")
     or FileName =~ ".env"
     or (FileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519","authorized_keys") and FolderPath has "/.ssh/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has "python" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","multiedit")
| where (TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/")
     or TargetFileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc")
     or (TargetFileName =~ "credentials" and TargetFilePath has "/.aws/")
     or TargetFileName =~ ".env"
     or (TargetFileName in~ ("id_rsa","id_ed25519") and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI multiedit secret-file read (/etc/shadow, id_rsa, .aws/credentials, .env) by python AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the read/exfil primitive of GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47: a python-hosted PraisonAI agent opening sensitive secret files via the unvalidated multiedit filepath (incl. dry_run diff leakage). Targets the exact files the advisory names — /etc/shadow, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, .env. Requires open/read telemetry (auditd watches or CrowdStrike FileOpenInfo) since Defender DeviceFileEvents does not emit read-only access. Rationale: Targets the precise secret paths the advisory cites as readable via the unvalidated multiedit tool, scoped to the python interpreter that hosts PraisonAI; defender_kql intentionally left empty because Defender DeviceFileEvents does not record read-only opens, so the detection leans on auditd/FileOpenInfo. Validated against the GHSA write-up and the PraisonAI advisory cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1003.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python automation reading its own project .env at startup (inside workspace)
  • Python-based config tooling reading ~/.aws/credentials during an authorized cloud operation
  • Backup/inventory agents written in Python touching /etc/shadow on a hardened host
  • Security scanners or compliance scripts (python) auditing shadow/SSH key permissions
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reader is PraisonAI (command line / parent contains praisonai|multiedit) and that the file is outside any legitimate workspace; check whether dry_run diff output of these files was returned to a chat/agent transcript. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the agent, and immediately rotate exposed secrets — SSH private keys, AWS access keys, anything in the read .env; force-expire AWS sessions. 3) Hunt: correlate the read timestamp with outbound python network connections (possible exfil) and with subsequent use of the leaked AWS keys in CloudTrail from new source IPs; check peer hosts running the same vulnerable PraisonAI build.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "type=PATH" or SyslogMessage has "type=SYSCALL" or ProcessName in ("audisp-syslog","auditd")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/shadow","/.ssh/id_rsa","/.ssh/id_ed25519","/.aws/credentials",".env")
| where SyslogMessage has "python"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI install/upgrade activity (verify version >= 4.6.61) AIWeaponization Low
Surfaces hosts where the vulnerable PraisonAI package (pip:praisonai < 4.6.61, fixed for GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) is being installed or upgraded, so exposure can be confirmed and patched. Exposure/hardening hunt rather than active-attack detection; pair with endpoint software inventory to confirm the resolved version. Rationale: Uses the advisory's concrete fixed-version boundary (praisonai 4.6.61) and package name to flag install/upgrade events for exposure triage; confidence is Low because it catches install commands (not container-baked images) and does not by itself prove the resolved version — confirm via software inventory/TVM. Cross-referenced with the GitHub Advisory fixed-version metadata. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patching activity that installs praisonai >= 4.6.61 (the safe version) — benign, the goal state
  • CI/CD build agents reinstalling dependencies including praisonai during normal pipeline runs
  • Developer creating a fresh virtualenv and pip-installing the project's requirements
  • Container image bake steps shown as process events on build hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: from the command line determine the requested version; then query endpoint software inventory / `pip show praisonai` on the host to get the actually-installed version and compare to 4.6.61. 2) Contain: if < 4.6.61, prioritize upgrade to >= 4.6.61; on internet-exposed or chatbot deployments using auto_approve_tools=True, restrict the multiedit tool or gate it behind approval until patched. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts/containers running praisonai (inventory + this query org-wide), then run the multiedit read/write UCs against those hosts to check for actual exploitation before the patch landed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip","pip3","python","python3","uv","poetry")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","upgrade","-U"," add ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3","uv","poetry")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","upgrade","-U"," add ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js MCP server reachable from public clients (unauthenticated MCPServer exposure) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core PraisonAI MCPServer flaw: startHttp() calls listen(port) with no host arg, binding to the unspecified address (observed '::') so the HTTP JSON-RPC transport is reachable on all interfaces. This surfaces Node listeners accepting inbound connections from public source IPs — the precondition for unauthenticated tools/call. Rationale: Targets the article's root cause — httpServer.listen(port) with no host binds to '::' (the PoV's observed bindAddress), making the MCP HTTP transport reachable off-host. Inbound-accept on node from a Public RemoteIP is the exposure that unauthenticated tools/call depends on. Cross-checked against GHSA-4qq2-2j2x-x62c and the Network-AI GHSA-fj4g-2p96-q6m3 (same '0.0.0.0 + no auth' MCP pattern) plus Censys-reported mass MCP exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-4qq2-2j2x-x62c/ • https://github.com/Jovancoding/Network-AI/security/advisories/GHSA-fj4g-2p96-q6m3 • https://www.anvilogic.com/threat-reports/mcp-server-auth-flaws
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internet-facing Node app (Express/Next.js) intentionally bound to 0.0.0.0 on the host
  • Public load-balancer / uptime-monitor health probes hitting the Node port
  • Dev server bound to all interfaces in a DMZ or cloud VM with a public IP
  • Reverse-proxy host where the Node origin legitimately serves external clients
  • Container/k8s node with NodePort service exposing the app publicly by design
Suppression filter
| where LocalPort !in (80, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the LocalPort and process — confirm whether it is the PraisonAI MCPServer (check the app's startup code for server.start({port}) / node_modules/praisonai) versus a sanctioned web app. Pull the RemoteIPs and check for non-business geographies/ASNs. 2) Contain: if it is an MCP server, restrict the listener to 127.0.0.1 (or firewall the port to trusted CIDRs) and front it with an authenticating reverse proxy; block the offending source IPs at the edge. 3) Hunt: pivot the same DeviceId into UC2 (child-process spawns by that node PID) and UC3 (tools/call request bodies) to determine whether tools were actually invoked.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 50) by DeviceName, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc

PraisonAI MCP server (node) spawns shell/LOLBin child after external connection AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts post-exploitation of the unauthenticated tools/call dispatcher: registered MCP tools commonly wrap code execution and run with the server process privileges. This correlates a Node listener accepting an inbound public connection with that same node PID spawning a command interpreter/LOLBin within 5 minutes — i.e. an unauthenticated caller driving server-side tool execution. Rationale: Maps the article's Impact section — tool handlers 'run with the server process privileges' and an unauthenticated caller can 'drive the same actions' including 'code execution.' The Defender variant ties the inbound public reach (server PID owning the socket) to a child spawn by the same PID, turning a noisy node→shell pattern into a high-fidelity unauth-RCE signal. Corroborated by GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj (unauthenticated workflow execution) and PraisonAI unauth-RCE via tool_override.py. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/praisonai/CVE-2026-44334/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / native module builds spawning cmd.exe during npm install
  • electron-builder or packaging tooling shelling out to powershell/cmd
  • CI/build agents running Node test runners that invoke shell scripts
  • pm2/forever/nodemon process managers spawning shells
  • Legitimately-registered MCP tools that are designed to run shell commands
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","electron-builder","npm-cli.js","node_modules\\.bin","prebuild-install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and the correlated RemoteIP/LocalPort — distinguish a build-tool shell (node-gyp/npm) from attacker commands (recon, download, encoded payloads). Confirm the parent node process is an MCP server. 2) Contain: kill the node MCP process, isolate the host, and rotate any server-side credentials/API keys the MCP tools had access to (they ran under the server identity). 3) Hunt: enumerate all tools/resources the server registered, review UC3 for the tools/call bodies that triggered execution, and sweep other hosts running the praisonai package for the same node→shell pattern.
let Window = 5m;
let InboundReach = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | project ConnTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, ServerPid=InitiatingProcessId, RemoteIP, LocalPort;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| join kind=inner InboundReach on DeviceId
| where InitiatingProcessId == ServerPid
| where Timestamp between (ConnTime .. ConnTime + Window)
| project ConnTime, SpawnTime=Timestamp, DelaySec=datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ConnTime), DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by ConnTime desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\curl.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI AgentOS Node server exposed to non-loopback on default port 8000 AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for a node.exe process accepting inbound network connections from non-loopback/public source addresses on TCP 8000, the configuration the advisory describes when AgentOS keeps its default host '0.0.0.0' and is started with serve({ port: 8000 }). This surfaces PraisonAI AgentOS instances that are network-reachable without authentication. Rationale: Anchors on the advisory's named defaults: AgentOS binds host '0.0.0.0' with no auth and the PoV/serve example listens on port 8000 via a node process. Inbound acceptance from a non-loopback source on node:8000 is the network signature of an internet/LAN-reachable unauthenticated AgentOS. Port is configurable so this is hunting-tier; cross-checked against the sibling Python AgentOS advisory and Sysdig's observation of internet-wide scanning of these instances. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892R-P3JQ-JP24 • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj

  • Legitimate internal Node/Express dev servers (webpack-dev-server, http-server, json-server) that also default to port 8000
  • Authorized internal access to a PraisonAI AgentOS instance that has been correctly fronted by auth/reverse proxy
  • Vulnerability scanners / Nessus / internal pentest sweeps probing 8000 across the estate
  • Containerized microservices that legitimately publish 8000 to the host network
  • Health-check or load-balancer probes to the listener from internal monitoring subnets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "agentos", "AgentOS") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "praisonai"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the listening process is PraisonAI by inspecting InitiatingProcessCommandLine / the node working directory for a node_modules/praisonai path, and identify whether SampleSources are internal or public. 2) Contain: if reachable from untrusted networks, firewall TCP 8000 to loopback/management only and restart AgentOS bound to 127.0.0.1, or place an authenticating reverse proxy in front. 3) Hunt: pull web/proxy logs for the same host to see whether /api/agents or /api/chat were actually hit (UC2), and review agent tool/credential scope for signs of abuse.

| where LocalPort == 8000
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where RemoteIPType != "Loopback" and RemoteIP != "127.0.0.1" and RemoteIP != "::1"

| order by LastSeen desc

| order by LastSeen desc

Unauthenticated PraisonAI AgentOS API hits: GET /api/agents enumeration + POST /api/chat invocation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects HTTP access to the AgentOS routes /api/agents (discloses agent names, roles and instruction prefixes) and /api/chat (invokes the agent without credentials) returning 200. Same source IP touching both endpoints, or the documented scanner User-Agent, indicates the read-then-invoke exploitation flow the advisory describes. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact route literals (apiPrefix default '/api' → /api/agents, /api/chat) and the 200-status fail-open behaviour (patched servers return 401). Requiring the same client to hit BOTH the enumeration and invocation routes encodes the read-then-invoke flow; the CVE-Detector/1.0 UA is the real scanner string Sysdig observed probing the identical endpoints on the sibling CVE-2026-44338. Defender XDR has no inbound-HTTP-request table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; FDR/Datadog likewise don't ship web access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892R-P3JQ-JP24 • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers or QA exercising /api/agents and /api/chat from a browser/Postman during testing
  • Application uptime monitors or synthetic transactions hitting both routes on a schedule
  • A correctly authenticated front-end legitimately calling both endpoints from one egress IP
  • Internal load testing tools generating GET+POST traffic to the AgentOS API
  • Security scanners other than CVE-Detector cataloguing the endpoints during an authorized assessment
Suppression filter
| where CIp !startswith "10." and CIp !startswith "192.168." and not (ipv4_is_in_range(CIp, "172.16.0.0/12"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether CIp is external/untrusted and whether the requests carried an Authorization header (check WAF/proxy header logs if available); a 200 on /api/chat from an external IP with no auth = confirmed unauthenticated invocation. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, take the AgentOS instance off untrusted networks, and rotate any credentials/tokens reachable by the invoked agent (env vars, downstream API keys). 3) Hunt: review the agent's tool/MCP/business-action logs for actions triggered in the request window, and pivot to UC1 to enumerate every exposed AgentOS listener in the estate.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsUriStem in~ ("/api/agents", "/api/chat")
| where ScStatus == 200
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(CsMethod), Endpoints = make_set(CsUriStem), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsHost
| extend Scanner = iff(UserAgents has "CVE-Detector/1.0", "yes", "no")
| where (set_has_element(Endpoints, "/api/agents") and set_has_element(Endpoints, "/api/chat")) or Scanner == "yes"
| order by LastSeen desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI npm package present (dist/os/agentos.js) on managed hosts AIInstallation High
Asset-exposure hunt for the affected component: the file dist/os/agentos.js dropped under a node_modules/praisonai path (shipped in npm praisonai >=1.6.0,<=1.7.1), or an 'npm install praisonai' command. Identifies which hosts actually carry the unauthenticated AgentOS code so they can be hardened before exploitation. Rationale: Deterministic article artifact: the advisory names the affected component path src/praisonai-ts/.../os/agentos.ts which ships as dist/os/agentos.js inside the npm praisonai tarball (boundary: <=1.5.4 did not ship dist/os). Matching agentos.js under a praisonai folder pins the exact vulnerable code on disk with near-zero ambiguity. Affected range >=1.6.0,<=1.7.1 confirmed in the advisory; the unauthenticated-by-default behaviour corroborated by the sibling AgentOS advisory GHSA-892R-P3JQ-JP24. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892R-P3JQ-JP24 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate, authorized PraisonAI deployment by an internal AI/ML team
  • CI/CD build agents that npm-install praisonai during pipeline runs
  • Developer workstations with the package in a local project's node_modules
  • Container image builds layering the package (file write seen at build time)
  • Security team intentionally staging the package for testing/reproduction
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed version (read package.json under the praisonai folder, or the InitiatingProcessCommandLine for an 'npm install praisonai@x'); flag any version in >=1.6.0,<=1.7.1. 2) Contain: ensure the AgentOS server is not started with the default host (bind 127.0.0.1), require an auth token, and firewall the listener; no fixed npm version existed at advisory time, so treat all installs as needing compensating controls. 3) Hunt: for each affected host, pivot to UC1 (is it listening on a non-loopback interface?) and UC2 (has anyone hit /api/agents or /api/chat?) to distinguish merely-installed from actively-exposed-and-probed.

PraisonAI codeMode sandbox-escape RCE: node process spawning OS shell / recon binaries AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a Node.js process running PraisonAI (praisonai-ts codeMode tool) spawning a shell, recon, or transfer binary. The codeMode sandbox is supposed to run JS in-process only; any child_process/execSync-spawned OS command from that node process is the direct manifestation of the Function-constructor blocklist bypass (GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84). The PoC literally ran `id` via cp.execSync. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact component (praisonai / codeMode) as the node parent plus a shell/recon child, because the sandbox is designed to run JS in-process only — a child OS process from it is the bypass executing. The PoC's `id` recon is included. Cross-checked GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp and CVE-2026-40158 which confirm child_process recovery via the Function constructor. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40158/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.004 T1033
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A PraisonAI deployment whose node command line legitimately invokes the python_tools subprocess sandbox (spawns python3)
  • Build/CI tooling running under the same node process tree (npm scripts, node-gyp, webpack) shelling out
  • Process managers like pm2/nodemon restarting and spawning sh
  • Container entrypoint scripts where node is PID 1 and forks a shell for health checks
  • Developer running node REPL with child_process during local testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("npm","node-gyp","yarn","webpack","install","healthcheck") and not (FileName =~ "python3" and ProcessCommandLine has "_execute_code_sandboxed")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ChildCmd and parent ParentCmd — confirm the parent node is actually running praisonai (check folder/cmdline) and the child is not a build/health-check script. Note the OS command run (id/whoami/curl indicate hands-on-keyboard). 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, kill the node process tree, and rotate any API keys/tokens/secrets present in that process's environment (env-var exfil is the stated impact). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/aid for outbound egress from node (UC3), for written persistence files, and confirm the praisonai version — upgrade to >=1.7.2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "praisonai"
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","node-gyp","yarn","webpack","install"))
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "ProcessCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai" or ActingProcessName has "praisonai"
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","node-gyp","yarn","webpack"))
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/bin/sh","/bin/bash","/bin/dash","/usr/bin/zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","/usr/bin/id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI codeMode component present on host (code-mode.ts/js under praisonai) AIReconnaissance High
Asset-discovery hunt for the vulnerable file path named in the advisory — src/praisonai-ts/src/tools/builtins/code-mode.ts (and its compiled code-mode.js) under any praisonai directory. Surfaces every host/container carrying the exploitable codeMode tool so they can be confirmed against the patched 1.7.2 release. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact vulnerable file path (src/praisonai-ts/src/tools/builtins/code-mode.ts) plus the compiled .js form to enumerate exposure. High confidence the file maps to the affected component; version confirmation (vs patched 1.7.2 from GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp) separates vulnerable from fixed. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84
ATT&CKT1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts running the PATCHED praisonai >=1.7.2 which still ships a code-mode file (fixed, not vulnerable) — verify package.json/version
  • Source-code mirrors, package caches, or git clones of praisonai-ts that are not actually executed
  • Security researchers' local checkout of the advisory PoC
  • Backup/restore images surfacing historical node_modules
  • Container image-build layers scanned by the EDR during CI
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, resolve the installed praisonai version (read package.json near the FolderPath or query the package manager) and whether codeMode is enabled for any agent. 2) Contain: on confirmed vulnerable (1.4.0–1.7.1) production hosts, disable the codeMode tool and/or upgrade to >=1.7.2; restrict the node process's egress and secrets exposure in the interim. 3) Hunt: correlate the host against UC1 (node spawning shells) and UC3 (node novel egress) to determine whether the vuln was merely present or actually exploited.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "praisonai"
| where FileName in~ ("code-mode.ts","code-mode.js")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), arg_max(Timestamp, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName) by DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "praisonai"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("code-mode.ts","code-mode.js")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

PraisonAI node process novel outbound egress (post-escape secret/API-key exfiltration or C2) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts a node process running PraisonAI making outbound connections to destinations outside the expected set of LLM/API/registry endpoints. After the codeMode escape, the stated impact is exfiltrating environment variables (API keys, tokens) and installing backdoors — both produce egress from the node process to attacker infrastructure not seen in a normal agent's API traffic. Rationale: Anchors on the praisonai node process (so it's article-specific, not generic node egress) and the advisory's named impact of env-var/API-key exfiltration and backdoor install. Excludes the normal LLM/API/registry endpoints an agent legitimately calls so residual hits are candidate exfil/C2. PraisonAI codeMode escape: Node.js process spawning OS shell for recon/secret access AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the post-escape behaviour of the PraisonAI codeMode sandbox break: a node host process spawning an OS shell (sh/bash/cmd/powershell) whose command line performs environment/credential/file recon. After `({}).constructor.constructor('return process')()` recovers `process.mainModule.require`, attacker code calls child_process to run commands the sandbox was meant to block. A node process that is only supposed to run 'sandboxed' JS should never shell out to read /etc/passwd, .env or printenv. Rationale: Uses the article's stated post-escape impact (child_process subprocess execution, reading env vars and host files) anchored on a node parent process — the one binary that hosts codeMode. Recon-token filter on the child command line keeps it from firing on every legitimate node->shell call. Cross-checked GHSA and the GitLab advisory mirror (fixed 1.7.2) plus public vm-escape write-ups showing the canonical execSync('cat /etc/passwd') payload. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://thegoodhacker.com/posts/the-unsecure-node-vm-module/ • https://github.com/vercel/workflow/issues/1026
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node app legitimately shelling out via child_process to git/imagemagick/ffmpeg during normal operation
  • npm/yarn lifecycle scripts (postinstall) invoking bash that runs uname/base64 during builds
  • node-gyp compiling native modules and reading system files
  • CI/CD runners using a node orchestrator to launch bash provisioning steps
  • Monitoring/backup agents written in Node that call whoami/hostname for inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","npm ","yarn ","prebuild","node_modules/.bin","/usr/lib/node_modules") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child command line and the node parent's command line/working dir; confirm whether this host runs a praisonai/codeMode agent endpoint and whether the recon target (.env, /etc/passwd, printenv) is legitimate for that service. 2) Contain: if unexplained, isolate the host, rotate any API keys/service tokens reachable from the node process environment, and quarantine the node service pending review. 3) Hunt: search the same host for sibling node->shell executions, outbound connections from node to new domains/IPs (exfil), and any process command line containing 'constructor.constructor' or 'process.mainModule.require'; pin the praisonai package version and upgrade to >=1.7.2.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","sh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow",".env","printenv","whoami","cat ","curl ","wget ","base64","child_process","uname","id ","hostname")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","sh.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow",".env","printenv","whoami","cat ","curl ","wget ","base64","child_process","uname")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI codeMode Function-constructor prototype-chain escape payload signature AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact JavaScript escape primitive used to break out of codeMode's fake sandbox: the prototype-chain recovery of the real Function constructor (`({}).constructor.constructor('return process')()`) combined with `process.mainModule.require`. When this payload transits a command line, application/syslog stream, or captured request body it is a near-zero-FP indicator of an attempted codeMode (or any Node vm/new Function) sandbox escape. Rationale: Targets the literal escape gadget the advisory documents (`({}).constructor.constructor('return process')()` -> `process.mainModule.require`), which the blocklist never covers; the two-token pairing (constructor.constructor + mainModule/return process) makes legitimate occurrence vanishingly rare. Datadog uses case-insensitive full-text phrase search so no casing enumeration is needed. Cross-checked against public Node vm/new Function escape research confirming the same gadget. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://thegoodhacker.com/posts/the-unsecure-node-vm-module/ • https://architecture.pub/articles/410978448.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SAST/dependency scanners or pentest tooling replaying the advisory PoC against your own apps
  • The PraisonAI regression/PoV test (poc/pov_poc.js) executing in CI or a developer sandbox
  • Security researchers or red team validating GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp in a lab
  • Application logs verbosely echoing a blocked/sanitised request body that contained the payload
  • Developer documentation or a blog/notebook about Node sandbox escapes being opened/built on the host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pov_poc.js","semgrep","trivy","grype","npm test","jest","mocha") or FolderPath has_any ("/poc/","\\test\\","/test/","node_modules"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full payload and its source (which process/log stream, which app endpoint, which user/IP submitted it) and determine whether it reached a live codeMode/vm sink or was logged after being blocked. 2) Contain: block the source IP/user at the agent/tool API, take the affected node service out of rotation, and rotate any secrets present in that process environment (API keys, service tokens). 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (node spawning shells) on the same host and time window, review outbound connections from the node process for exfil, confirm praisonai is patched to >=1.7.2, and audit other tool endpoints that funnel user/LLM content into new Function or vm.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "constructor.constructor"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("return process","return this.process","mainModule","process.mainModule","child_process")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage contains "constructor.constructor"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("mainModule","return process","return this.process","child_process")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

INC Ransomware BYOVD vulnerable driver drop (filwfp.sys / filnk.sys / fildds.sys) AIInstallation High
Hunts the file write or load of the three named vulnerable kernel drivers INC ransomware affiliates use to blind EDR/AV before encryption. These filenames are not legitimate Windows or vendor drivers, so any appearance is high-fidelity; Sophos observed all three loaded onto one network within seven minutes. Rationale: Uses the three exact BYOVD driver filenames from the article, independently confirmed by Sophos X-Ops (three loads in 7 minutes on one network). No legitimate driver carries these names, so a bare file-create match is high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://x.com/SophosXOps/status/1764933957286855058 • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/what-are-bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver-byovd-attacks
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher detonating INC samples in a sanctioned malware lab
  • EDR/AV vendor signature test files staged under a quarantine folder
  • Threat-intel team copying captured driver samples to a forensic share
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Sandbox\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess that wrote the .sys file and whether the host is a backup/edge server; check for a same-host service-create or driver-load event seconds later. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately and block the driver hash org-wide; INC drops these only minutes before mass encryption. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing process tree for prior Veeam credential access, rclone exfil, and RMM (AnyDesk/ScreenConnect/TeamViewer) installs across the estate.
DeviceFileEvents

| where FileName in~ ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp asc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFileName in~ ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated asc

INC Rust encryptor launched with --esxi hypervisor argument AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of a process invoked with INC ransomware's documented '--esxi' command-line flag, which triggers the Rust encryptor to shut down running virtual machines before encrypting ESXi datastores. Targets Linux/ESXi hosts where Defender for Endpoint or auditd telemetry is available. Rationale: The '--esxi' operator flag that drives the encryptor to power off VMs is stated verbatim in the article and corroborated by Acronis/CybersecurityNews reporting on the Rust Linux/ESXi variant. It is an unusual token rarely seen in benign command lines. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/inc-ransomware-uses-rust-based-windows/amp/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/inc-ransomware-thrives-by-mastering-the-basics
ATT&CKT1486 T1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin VM-migration or DR scripts that pass an --esxi parameter to an internal tool
  • Backup/replication jobs invoking ESXi automation with a similar flag
  • Security testing of ESXi-targeting tooling in a lab cluster
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("/usr/lib/vmware", "/opt/vmware")) and FileName !in~ ("vim-cmd", "esxcli", "vmware-vim-cmd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary is unsigned/unknown and not a sanctioned VMware utility; check the host for simultaneous mass VM power-off (vim-cmd / esxcli vm process kill). 2) Contain: power-isolate the ESXi host from management/storage networks and snapshot datastores if not yet encrypted. 3) Hunt: review the host for the BYOVD driver drops, rclone exfil, and lateral RDP/PsExec inbound from the same operator account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--esxi"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--esxi" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "--esxi"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated asc

INC Ransomware Rclone cloud exfiltration of staged archives AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts INC's data-theft step: rclone (or a renamed rclone identified by its characteristic flags) copying/syncing data to an external cloud remote after the operator stages it as password-protected archives. Catches both the named binary and renamed copies via flag fingerprinting. Rationale: Rclone is the exfiltration tool named in the article; the renamed-binary fallback fingerprints rclone's distinctive --config/--transfers/--multi-thread-streams flags so a rename to evade the binary-name match still fires. Pairs with the article's password-protected-archive staging (T1560.001). Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/inc-ransomware-thrives-by-mastering-the-basics
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/backup teams using rclone for legitimate cloud backup or migration
  • DevOps syncing artifacts to S3/B2/GDrive via rclone in CI
  • Personal-use rclone on a developer workstation copying to a cloud remote
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "backup-agent.exe") and AccountName !startswith "svc-backup"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the rclone command line for the remote target and source path; cloud destinations (mega/b2/onedrive) sourcing from file shares or backup volumes are high risk. 2) Contain: block the destination domain/IP at egress, suspend the executing account, and preserve the rclone config (often holds the attacker's remote creds). 3) Hunt: look for 7-Zip/WinRAR/rar processes creating password-protected (-p/-hp) archives on the same host just before, and correlate with BYOVD driver drops signalling imminent encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "rclone.exe"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--config"
       and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--transfers", "--multi-thread-streams", "--no-check-certificate", "--ignore-existing")
       and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("copy", "sync", "move"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rclone.exe"
   or (CommandLine has "--config"
       and (CommandLine has "--transfers" or CommandLine has "--multi-thread-streams" or CommandLine has "--no-check-certificate")
       and (CommandLine has "copy" or CommandLine has "sync" or CommandLine has "move"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated asc

INC Veeam backup credential dumping (salted DPAPI SQL secret access) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts INC's updated credential dumper reading Veeam Backup & Replication's stored SQL credentials (SqlLogin / SqlSecuredPassword DPAPI blobs) or the VeeamBackup Credentials table from a non-Veeam process on a backup server. Targets the credential-access step that lets INC neutralize recovery before encryption. Rationale: Anchors on Veeam's real credential-store internals — the SqlLogin/SqlSecuredPassword DPAPI registry values under 'Veeam Backup and Replication' and the VeeamBackup [Credentials] table — which the article's salted-DPAPI Veeam dumper must touch; the non-Veeam-parent filter keeps it focused on the attacker tool, not the product itself. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://securitybrief.com.au/story/inc-ransomware-surges-as-australia-stays-in-sights
ATT&CKT1003 T1555 T1552.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam admins running official credential-migration or upgrade scripts
  • Backup-monitoring tooling querying the VeeamBackup config DB
  • DBA running ad-hoc SELECTs against the VeeamBackup database during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("veeamadmin", "svc-veeam") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sqlservr.exe", "postgres.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the executing binary/account is not a sanctioned Veeam component or admin; review whether it ran on a designated backup server. 2) Contain: rotate all credentials stored in Veeam (service, repository, vCenter/ESXi, cloud) and isolate the backup server, since dumped creds enable backup deletion and lateral movement. 3) Hunt: trace the operator account to inbound RDP/RMM sessions, look for backup-job or repository deletion, and the BYOVD driver drops that precede INC encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "Veeam Backup and Replication" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SqlSecuredPassword", "SqlLogin"))
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "VeeamBackup" and ProcessCommandLine has "Credentials")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Veeam.Backup.Manager.exe", "Veeam.Backup.Service.exe", "Veeam.Backup.PowerShell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "Veeam Backup and Replication" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("SqlSecuredPassword", "SqlLogin"))
     or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "VeeamBackup" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "Credentials")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("Veeam.Backup.Manager.exe", "Veeam.Backup.Service.exe", "Veeam.Backup.PowerShell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated asc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp

| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),

| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| order by conn_count desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-3519", "CVE-2025-5777", "CVE-2023-48788", "CVE-2024-57727")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-3519", "CVE-2025-5777", "CVE-2023-48788", "CVE-2024-57727")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:

            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
